utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, let us see. I see that we have a listing of distances and driving times. I had indicated yesterday that I would ask you some questions regarding that. When I have time to look at it, I will see whether they satisfy all of my needs. My real concern was for distances from Prijedor, but we will pass that for the moment. I did have some questions regarding counts 5 through 11. I do not know that I can really ask you all of the questions at this point, because we received the transcript for the afternoon session rather late and I have not had a chance to go through it thoroughly. But I did want to pose a few questions to you at this time, not for you to answer at this time, perhaps after we have had an opportunity to look at the transcript, you may be able to either tell me that you told me the answer to the question, or perhaps there will be more questions. The first question is as follows: did Ferid Mujcic identify the accused as calling out Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can answer that. The answer to that is he said that he saw the accused when Karabasic was called out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He saw the accused when Karabasic was called out. Then regarding Velic's testimony, comparing it with Besic's testimony, Velic, I believe, describes the calling out of Hrnic and he says, I believe, that he saw the accused after a guard had opened the door. Besic, I believe, testified that he saw the accused personally call out Hrnic. Now I may be mistaken about that, but that is my understanding and that is something I would like you to clear up. The other question is, is there any evidence from any of the eight, I guess, witnesses who testified that any of them saw the beating of Mr. Alic? The next question relates to Mr. Grozdanic. He testified that he saw two bodies, but he also testified that he saw Hrnic called out and I believe he testified that he saw military police calling out for Hrnic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, his testimony in that regard was that as he went back to his room, as he approached the room, he saw a person he described as a military policeman outside the room and Hrnic coming out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, but did not ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because as he came there, he actually saw Hrnic exit the room. We will check that further, but my recollection of his testimony, he did not say who had called him out but he saw what he described as a military policeman at the door as he saw Hrnic come out the door.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then a question as it relates to Mr. Hodzic: I believe he testified that Mr. Karabasic was called out when he was close to him. They were in the same room and they were upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: His testimony, I believe, your Honour, was that Emir Karabasic was about three people away from him and his regular place in the room was about three people away from Husein Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the upstairs room?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the upstairs room, your Honour, in B14.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then just by way of chronology, let me ask you whether this fits with your understanding of the testimony in terms of the victims being called out. First, Mr. Alic, Mehmed Alic, was on his way from lunch and the accused was outside the hangar on one side of the pista wearing a camouflage uniform. Then, as it relates to Mr. Mujcic, as the accused entered the hangar with the group wearing camouflage uniforms he saw the accused. They were not camp guards but they came from outside the camp. Then Mr. Kenjar: the accused was on the floor of the hangar wearing a camouflage uniform some time before the calling out of the victims. Then Mr. Besic: in the late afternoon the accused was being -- he saw him as actually engaged in calling out Hrnic, telling him to come out or the others in the room would be killed. Then Mr. Mujcic saw the accused in a camouflage uniform standing behind a guard who had opened the door of his room in the hangar and was calling out Karabasic. We have talked about that; and again by Velic who saw the accused momentarily in the door of his room when Hrnic was called out. There the accused was wearing a camouflage uniform; and by Halid Mujkanovic, at the time of the beating of the three the accused was standing on the floor of the hangar but not involved in the beating. Then by Grozdanic, had seen the accused in the morning when he was accosted and briefly questioned by the accused on the floor of the hangar. Again the accused was wearing a camouflage uniform, and he saw him sometime later while the accused was beating unidentified prisoners on the hangar floor. I guess that is rather confusing, but I have some questions again about the calling out and where was the accused at the time and whether there is any inconsistency between Velic and Besic and Mr. Mujcic. Those are really the ones. We can follow it up later, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to Mehmed Alic, his testimony indicated he was on his way to lunch when he saw the accused, as did Husein Hodzic. They were on their way to get their one meal of the day when they saw the accused. Armin Mujcic testified that in the afternoon when he was seated on that bench, you will recall he had dysentery and sat on the bench, he saw the accused and the group coming into the hangar. So as for those two, that is the testimony that they provided. We will check the transcript and the other evidence for the other questions that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note in response also to your discussion about those distances and times that we have shown those to the Defence and they are in agreement with those. As you will see, basically what we did was went back through the transcript and the testimony and tried to pull out the distances and times as the witnesses gave them. One final note before I proceed to the next counts ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me talk to you then about the distances. Do you have listed Prijedor to Kozarac, the distance?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Kozarac to Prijedor, and that would be what, from 10 to 15 kilometres, 10 to 11, and 11 kilometres. OK. Prijedor to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, 22. Prijedor to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have Kozarac to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, we do. Banja Luka to Prijedor, we have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It would be the next one down from Banja Luka, the distances. It is the very first entry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then Prijedor to Jaskici and Sivci?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Prijedor to Jaskici, that I do not believe we have. We have Kozarac, we have Kozarac to Jaskici, but we do not have ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Jaskici is to the south east, is it -- south west? I am trying to determine whether we could calculate that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: South east.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you have from Kozarac to Jaskici?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think you should, your Honour; there may be a more direct route ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I was thinking anyway.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- but you have Prijedor to Kozarac and then from Kozarac to Jaskici is three to three-and-a-half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The maps do not show any more direct route?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, and given the location of that very small hamlet, there is basically a track that you took to get there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have Kozarac to Jaskici?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I have no further questions now regarding distances. You may continue, unless you have something else preliminary?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. One additional matter: in checking the transcript last evening, I noticed a one word difference in what I thought I had said and what the transcript indicated I had said. In my mind, it is a difference of significance so I would like to clarify if I misspoke. When I was discussing why this accused is criminally liable for all of the crimes that were committed in the hangar that day, what I had intended to say was that although the evidence that you have does not establish that the accused was the member of the group who ordered G to emasculate Fikret Harambasic, he, nonetheless, was criminally liable for that act. The reason I make that difference is that on page 6593 of the transcript it says that he was not a member of the group. To me that is a difference with some significance. So I point it out to you. We do believe that there are facts in the record that certainly establish that at the time he continued to be a member of that group but, indeed, the evidence does not establish he was the person who gave the order for that emasculation to be carried out. Your Honours, if I could turn to the next counts, and here I will deviate from the order of the counts, and I want to talk with you about the evidence concerning counts 12 to 14 and 21 to 23. I will speak first of counts 21 to 23 which allege crimes by this accused in the beating of Hase Icic. Then chronologically following that was the beating of Sefik Sivac which is the subject of counts 12 to 14. So, to keep it in chronological order, I wish to speak about 21 to 23 first. These counts charge that by his acts he inflicted great suffering or cruel treatment or committed an inhumane act against these witnesses. As for the beating of Hase Icic, 21 to 23, the accused's act here was a part of the overall campaign of terror and intimidation that began against this witness when this victim and others were first brought to the White House. At that time you will recall Hase Icic told you they were made to lie on the floor with their hands out in the three finger Serb salute position. They were then beaten and crosses were carved into their clothing or, with some of them, into their skin. Later, Krkan (who was identified as a shift Commander at the camp and one who took people out) came to the room where Hase Icic was and told everyone in that room that they had to give up their money and whatever valuables they had, and that they had to write their names on a list and next to their name they should write what valuables and what money they were providing. He indicated that if they gave enough, then they would be spared any further torture. The men in that room had nothing to give, so they did, in fact, put their names on a list but there was nothing next to their name to show any contribution. Krkan returned to the room and took the list and left the room. That night, when the men were taken to a small room at the end of the corridor and beaten, they were called out in the same order their names appeared on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are missing the transcript. We do not have a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That night, Icic heard men saying that the "executioners" were coming. He was sitting by the door of his room in the White House and saw the accused and five other men all in uniform. Among the other five, in addition to the accused, he knew a Serb named Kevic. He also recognised two men that he had seen come to Keraterm while he was held there, men that had been called Duca and Banovic. There was another man with them that the executioners themselves called Babic when they talked to him. Krkan, this shift Commander, was also with the group. The accused and the other Serbs set up lighting in the hallway and it was with the assistance of this lighting that Hase Icic was able to see what was happening in the hallway. Then the Serbs began to bring out prisoners again in the same order they had signed their names on that list they had made earlier. Icic observed as a man who would be called out and taken to the small room at the end of the hallway, then he heard sounds of beating but no screams or cries. Some time later Icic would see the beaten prisoner brought back out of that small room at the end of the hallway and then taken to another room. After 10 or 15 men had been taken out and beaten in this fashion, the beaters took a break. They went outside the White House drinking and toasting and calling each other by their names. They divided up tasks by their specialities. Then refreshed, they came back in and continued with their task. If you will look at the overhead monitor, this is a photograph of the room at the end of the hallway to which these men were taken and eventually to which Hase Icic was taken when his turn came. When he entered that room, a noose was put around his neck and tightened to the point that he had no air. The accused and the other Serbs then savagely beat him, using all types of objects. As a result of this beating, he lapsed in and out of consciousness throughout, only regaining full consciousness in the morning. At that time he was in a different room with other beaten men. A guard came in to take out the dead bodies and those that were unconscious and stepped on Icic who cried out in pain. For that reason, because he had evoked a response from Icic, Icic was not carried out with the dead or unconscious. Was it this accused who committed those acts? Hase Icic saw the accused there with five other Serbs. Icic knew the accused since Icic was in school. The accused in his group put lighting in the hallway which enabled Icic to see the accused and the others. The accused was face to face with Icic when Icic was taken out into that small room and beaten. When the accused and the other Serbs took a break, they were outside the White House addressing each other by their names, including "Dule". The evidence establishes that this accused committed those crimes. Did the accused intend by his acts to cause great suffering or serious bodily injury? Again the acts that were committed can be used to prove this accused's intent and looking at those acts his intent is clear. Taking part in putting a noose around someone's neck, tightening it until they cannot breathe, loosening it only so that they could maintain consciousness to be more aware of the beating that was inflicted on them, at the same time the victim is savagely beaten with a whip, with an iron rod, with a wooden bat, with special rubber sticks, all the time while this noose is tight around their neck, this is intent to cause great suffering or serious bodily injury. In addition to that, as this victim continued to slip in and out of consciousness, the beatings continued. Looking at that beating itself, in the light of the conditions at Omarska camp, the regular beatings that took place there, the other beatings that this accused was involved in there, and remembering what Krkan told the men, "If you give enough money and other valuables, it will save you from further torture", satisfies this requirement. There is proof beyond a reasonable of the requisite intent. Was great suffering or serious bodily harm caused? The evidence proves this element as well. The beating caused the victim to repeatedly lose consciousness. The next morning he came to in a room of men who were either battered unconscious or dead. The guard who came in to collect the dead stepped on the accused, and when Icic responded with a cry of pain, the guard noted that Icic was alive but not for long. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty of counts 21 to 23. As for counts 12 to 14, the beating of Sefik Sivac, that beating resulted in Sefik Sivac's death, again the evidence proves that the accused is guilty of this offence. Within one or two days of the savage beating of Hase Icic, the accused participated in the fatal beating of Sefik Sivac. This beating also occurred at night. Was it the accused who committed this beating? The evidence proves that it was. Sivac was beaten one or two nights after the accused and others beat Hase Icic. On that night, before the accused and another man appeared outside the door to Icic's room, Icic heard sounds of beating outside. When the accused appeared in the White House that night, Icic was again near the doorway to his room facing the door with his head and shoulders partly on someone's else legs. The hallway was lit with lighting from some source enabling Icic to see what was happening in the hallway. Icic recognised the accused as one of the two men who dragged Sivac to the room and then threw him in a heap at Icic's feet. In addition to that, if we look at the overall plan to rid opstina Prijedor of non-Serbs through killings or otherwise, the evidence proves it was the accused who committed this act because the accused had a personal motive, had a personal reason, to beat Sivac. The words that Icic heard the accused speak become clear in that context, because he heard the accused say, "you see, Sivac, you cannot touch a Serb or say anything to a Serb". Did the accused intend to cause great suffering or serious injury? Again the acts themselves prove his intent to do so. Husein Hodzic also gave you evidence of this intent because he told you when he saw the body, the dead body, of Sefik Sivac the next day, the clothes were all torn, the body was bloody. It was a body but did not look like a body. The nature of the injuries inflicted on Sefik Sivac also prove the intent that was involved in this beating. You will recall that when he was thrown into the room, Hase Icic, because it was dark in the room, did not know who the man was but he heard the man ask for water. When water was given to him, he was in such a bad state he could not even drink the water that he had been asking for. In addition to that, the proof of intent is the words that Icic heard from the accused when he threw the body into the room: "You see, Sivac, you cannot touch a Serb or say anything to a Serb". What was he talking about? He was talking about the testimony you heard here of the incident before these attacks began in opstina Prijedor when Sefik Sivac forced the accused to leave his restaurant Deluxe after a heated political argument. You recall he forced him to leave. He ejected him from the restaurant. You will recall that when the accused was leaving he told them what would happen: "There will be a greater Serbia, it will be ours, and you will not be here any more". Not only did he have the motivation of carrying out the persecution that was ongoing in this opstina, he had the personal motivation of revenge upon a person who threw him out of a cafe or a restaurant. You recall Sofia Tadic telling you this accused was quite willing and capable of carrying out violence upon people with whom he had disagreements. Was great suffering or serious injury caused? Again the evidence proves that it was. The fact that he was unable to drink, the fact that, in fact, he died of this beating, the condition of his body the next day, all of this proves that, in fact, great suffering, serious injury, was occasioned by this beating. The accused has presented no evidence to establish an alibi for these offences. You will recall that Hase Icic told you that he was brought to Omarska on either 7th or 8th July. He was not sure about the date, he thought the 7th or 8th July. If we look at the police schedule for July, Defence Exhibit 64C, if it can be considered accurate at all, it shows that the accused was not working the night of the 7th of July, the night of 8th July, nor was he working the night of 10th July. On the 9th July he is shown to be working from 1900 hours to 0700 hours the following morning. That schedule does not preclude him from taking part in the fatal beating of Sefik Sivac for the reasons I have discussed earlier. The accused would have had no difficulty to leave his post, to carry out his greater duties, that is, the continuing persecution of non-Serbs in opstina Prijedor, with the full support and participation of the police. This is especially true when you recall there was a curfew in place from 2100 hours to 0600 hours and that curfew was in place every night. His presence would not have been required at this checkpoint where his only authority was over civilian vehicles during hours when there would have been no civilian vehicles. The evidence proves beyond reasonable doubt that the accused's guilt of counts 12 to 14. Now if I could turn to counts 15 to 17. You recall these counts involve the infliction of great suffering, serious injury, cruel treatment or inhumane acts arising from the beating of Hakija Elezovic and others behind the White House at Omarska. The evidence of Hakija Elezovic and Samir Hodzic prove those counts beyond reasonable doubt. Their evidence is consistent in all significant aspects. Both men place the accused in Omarska at the White House when Salih Elezovic, Sejad Sivac and others were killed. They both tell of Serbs forcing them and other Muslim men from their homes near Trnopolje on 9th July and being taken in a column to Trnopolje. The column of Hakija and the column of Samir joined up somewhere along the route. They both testified to people being taken out of the column and killed. Hakija watched as his younger son was shot a few metres from where Hakija stood. Samir's uncle was taken out of the column and a few metres later on Samir heard shots and he has never seen his uncle since. Both men were taken from Trnopolje to Omarska, then from Omarska on to Keraterm because Omarska was full. They were held at Keraterm about 10 days, Samir Hodzic tells you, until about 20th July. Hakija told you about his interrogation there at Keraterm by the director of the Kozarac National Park and about the accused's presence during that interrogation and the accused at that time also beating Hakija Elezovic. Hakija Elezovic and Samir Hodzic were transferred together to Omarska and were put in the same room there, that small room at the end of the corridor in the White House, that same small room that had been the room where Hase Icic and others had been beaten. Upon arrival at Omarska, the men told you they had to lean up against the wall with their fingers raised in the three finger position and they were beaten at that time. While Hakija was at Omarska, he told you that he saw his son once on the pista but was unable to talk to him. As to the events of the day when Hakija and the others were beaten, Hakija told you that he was taken for interrogation twice on that day, and that he and Samir were still in the same room at the White House, the small room at the end of the hallway. Samir told you that on that day while they were both in that small room at the end of the hallway he saw Hakija Elezovic taken out for interrogation twice. He told you that after Hakija was taken out the second time, he never saw Hakija again. Hakija told you that when he was called out for interrogation, he was beaten when he first arrived so that he had blood in his mouth. He was unable to talk. He was eventually sent back to the White House. When he was sent back the second time and came to the top of the stairs, the same man who had interrogated him at Keraterm, Radakovic, was there and that he and some military met Hakija at the top of those stairs and Radakovic said, "Oh, you are back to get it" and hit Hakija causing Hakija to fall down. Hakija was then taken back to the White House, but instead of being taken into the White House, he was taken around to the back of the White House. As he turned to corner to the back of the White House, the accused and several other Serbs were there beating men who were behind the White House. Hakija told you there were many men back there. Some of them looked as though they were dead already. Others were being beaten. Hakija saw his son behind the White House. As he turned the corner the accused met him there and the accused said, "Now you have come to the right place", and the accused began to beat Hakija using those same kinds of kicks he had used in Keraterm, the kicks that Hakija Elezovic described to you as those master's kicks, the kind he had seen in judo and karate movies. As he was beating Hakija Elezovic, Hakija's son, Salih, cried out to let his father alone. At that time the accused then stopped beating Hakija and went after Salih with a pistol and Salih fell. Then Hakija Elezovic told you that he was struck a very severe blow and was knocked unconscious. In the meantime, Samir Hodzic and his friend Zuhdija Turkanovic were transferred from that small room at the end of the corridor to another room in the White House and, subsequently, Samir himself was called out for interrogation. When he was brought back to the White House, a guard called him over to the corner of the White House, the corner nearest the restaurant building. The guard asked where Samir was from and how old he was, and Samir told him. At that time Samir saw the accused there with several other Serbs sitting in uniform, sitting on a bench, leaning up against the side of the White House. Samir was then told to go and sit about 10 metres away, sitting facing the accused and the other people at the White House. As he was sitting there, the guard asked him again where he was from and then took Samir Hodzic around the front of the White House to the other side of the White House, the side closest to the hangar, took him around to the rear side of the White House there, and there Samir Hodzic saw four bodies piled faced down, one on top of the other. The guard told him to turn the bodies over. As Samir turned the bodies over, they fell off each other in a row and Samir recognised the four men, Salih Elezovic, Senad or Sejad Sivac, a veterinarian from Sivci who had come to Samir's home, Redzep Causevic, whom Samir had met during his detention, and a man named Arslanovic, a neighbour and a friend of Samir Hodzic. He saw injuries on the men. On Salih Elezovic, he saw a wound below his chin either from a knife or a bullet. The guard asked Samir Hodzic if he knew these men. Samir lied and said he did not. At some point in this, he took the shoes off the body of Salih Elezovic. He stepped back. He was told to leave and he went to the White House. When he testified to you, he said not once did he look behind the White House. Sejad Sivac, the veterinarian from Sivci, had been in the hangar with his good friend Ermin Strikovic when he was taken out for the last time. Sejad had been beaten previously and had just recovered from that beating when he was taken out again. He gave his personal belongings to his friend Ermin and Ermin saw him kicked in the chest as Sejad left the room. Ermin knew he would not see his friend again and asked around to determine the time and the date, and he noted 27th July, 1420 hours, as the time that Sejad Sivac was taken out. Not long after Samir Hodzic had returned to his new room in the White House, having seen these four corpses, his friend Zuhdija Turkanovic was brought back into the room. Zuhdija was in pain and Samir tried to comfort him, putting Zuhdija's head on Samir's legs, trying to make him more comfortable. Some minutes later, Zuhdija Turkanovic died. Maybe 10 to 15 minutes after that, Zuhdija was taken out of the room. Later that day, Samir heard the sound of a truck nearby. Hakija Elezovic regained consciousness and saw Samir Hodzic with Salih. He saw Samir take his son's shoes. Hakija remembers that Samir was loading the bodies and that Samir took Salih and Sivac. Hakija remembers that he told Samir he could have Salih's shoes. He remembers Samir and another man taking him back into the White House. Hakija saw his son's body close to him and he saw the bodies of others as well. He saw Sivac, the veterinarian, and others he knew. As he remembers it, he saw the bodies piled on top of each other. He also saw the body of Zuhdija Turkanovic. He told you there were many bodies behind the White House. They loaded a truck full of them. When Hakija was taken from Omarska camp, when that camp was closed, he was taken to Trnopolje. When Samir was taken from Omarska camp, when that camp was closed, he was taken to Manjaca. The evidence of this count proves the accused's guilt. Hakija Elezovic and Samir Hodzic corroborate each other in every significant aspect -- up until what time? Up until the time that Hakija Elezovic was struck that severe blow on the back of his head knocking him unconscious. Both Hakija and Samir say the accused was there at the time of the incident. Both Hakija and Samir say that the accused had on a camouflage uniform. Hakija says that he saw the accused go after his son with a pistol. Samir says there was a wound below Salih's chin either from a knife or a bullet. Samir told you that he never looked behind the White House. So, Hakija's testimony about other bodies there is not contradicted by Samir. So why the differences after Hakija is knocked unconscious? As a result of the severe blow to the neck, Hakija was in such a deep state of unconsciousness that he was stabbed in the leg with no apparent reaction. He in his testimony rightly attributes his state of unconsciousness to his ability to survive the beatings and the murders that occurred there that day. He was mistakenly left for dead. Because it is not unusual, it is something you do not have to be a doctor to know, that such a severe blow can cause disorientation, can cause confusion about the timing of what you see and, put in that context, it is clear that there is no significant deviation in the testimony of Hakija Elezovic and of Samir Hodzic. You recall Samir Hodzic told you that he had to turn the bodies over, to turn them face up. Hakija Elezovic comes out of consciousness for a time, what does he see? He sees Samir Hodzic there turning the bodies over. He sees Samir Hodzic take the shoes off. Is it not reasonable for him to assume that he is turning the bodies over and going to load them because they are dead, because later when he regains consciousness he does see people loading bodies. This is confusion caused by the severe blow to the back of the head, the severe blow that occurred after Hakija Elezovic saw the accused there, was beaten by the accused there, saw the other men there, saw the accused beat his son Salih. This, we suggest, is the reasonable explanation for where the deviation occurs after the events Hakija Elezovic's testifies to. Hakija's recognition of the accused and how he came to match the accused's face with the name is very reasonable and very realistic, and indicates that indeed it was the accused that inflicted this beating on Hakija Elezovic and on Hakija's son. During testimony, Samir Hodzic was questioned about an earlier statement in which he had given a description of the accused. His explanation for that earlier statement was reasonable as well, especially in light of the difficulties we know exist when it comes to translation and interpretation. Basically, what Samir Hodzic told you was he saw the accused and when he saw the accused the accused was suntanned or sunburned. He was darker than he had seen him before. When he had seen him before, the accused was pale. This certainly would be reasonable in light of the fact that during these activities the accused has been engaged in during this hot summer, he has been outside, he would be suntanned. He could very possibly be sunburned. Samir also told you that the accused's hair was dark, going to dark, that it was lighter but it was going to dark, lightened by the sun. That too is not an unreasonable explanation. Samir told you in this courtroom, "I gave the same definition, the same description, I am giving now". Again, taken in context and taken in the light of what we know are difficulties with interpretation, that is not an unreasonable statement by this witness. It is not an incredible statement by this witness. When you review the evidence on this charge and you review it in the light of the reasonable explanations, it is unfortunate but true that Hakija was there that day to see his older son beaten by the accused and to later see his son's body. But perhaps these two witnesses got together and made up this story. If they did, they did not do it so well in the courtroom because they both testified in variance with each other. In addition to that, Samir Hodzic told you that from the time Hakija Elezovic left that room he did not see him until 1996. They were not refugees in the same country. If Hakija Elezovic wanted to make up his story, to hold this accused guilty because Serbs had killed his sons, then why did he not put the accused at the death of his earlier son as well? He could have done that; it would have made it even more convincing for you . They did not do that because they did not make up their stories because they told you the facts as they witnessed them, as they experienced them. The inconsistencies that are there are inconsistencies that are understandable. The Defence evidence offers no alibi for this crime either. Ermin Strikovic again told you that it was on 27th July, it was in the afternoon, when his friend was taken out for the last time. Even if you accept the schedules as accurate, Defence Exhibit 64 shows you that the accused was not working on that date. On 26th and 28th, he was working from 1900 to 0700 hours which meant he was free during the day which is when this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think on 27th he went to work at 7.00 p.m., did he not? Let us see if we can find it. At least the Defence's submission regarding the chronological schedule of alibi indicates that he went to work at 1900.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, which leaves him free during the day to commit these offences.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that, but I did not understand that that was the information that you gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have some questions to ask you about these counts or this count. The first one is the date of the occurrence; you get that not from the evidence of the two main witnesses to it, but from whose evidence?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the evidence of Ermin Strikovic who was a very good friend of Sejad Sivac. When Sejad was taken out that last time, he noted the time and the date because he was certain that he would never see his friend again. It is from that evidence that we get the 27th and the time. The other witnesses were not aware of ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, they were not. I wonder if you can sometime give me a page reference to that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and I believe that was also in the materials that were given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We will get that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. Then I wanted to ask you, you must surely have come across the statement by Elezovic in cross-examination in which he says, "In Keraterm it was Dusko who beat me, not in Omarska". Have you any comments on that statement?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think that was a question, as I recall, about Radakovic and if Radakovic was involved in beatings. I think that was in response to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is how you would explain it?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is my recollection of that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And, what, "Dusko" is Radakovic's first name, you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour. "Dusko", he was talking about Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. He says, "In Keraterm it was Dusko who beat me, not in Omarska".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I think again it was in response to a question about Radakovic. I think that the witness's answer was a confused answer because of the question. Hakija Elezovic says throughout his testimony that, in fact, it was Dusko Tadic who did beat him and he recognised him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Of course we have all the problems of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then the next thing I wanted to ask you about was where Hodzic says that he would have seen anything behind the White House, had there been anything there to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Then the follow up question to that is ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: He did not look behind.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The follow up question was something to the effect, yes, "How long did you look behind? What did you see?" He said, "I never looked behind the White House".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So this again is a matter of some interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Some interpretation, but I believe when he was asked more specifically that he indicated he never looked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then what about the curiosity that Hodzic says nothing about hearing of what must have been very prolonged the beating and killing of 50 or 60 men just behind the White House?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It may not have been that prolonged. Some of them were dead Hakija says when he went back there. Hakija had been taken out for interrogation. The beatings were, perhaps, not heard. You recall shortly after Hakija went out for interrogation, Samir Hodzic was removed to another room in the White House.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But he was still in this small White House?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right. The fact that the beatings were occurring back there and they did not hear them, I think is perhaps in the context of so many things going on at Omarska at the time that it would not necessarily have been something they paid attention to until the shots, if there were shots fired and people were killed. You will recall that Samir Hodzic was taken for interrogation, and when he came back then he found the bodies in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The four bodies?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the page cite in the transcript for Ermin Strikovic is 2872 to 73 where he talks about the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hodzic, though, would put this time as an estimate for July 20th, does he not?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour. He says that is when they left Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is when they left Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I misunderstood. When he was at Keraterm, then that was Radakovic -- did he testify that he though Mr. Tadic was his bodyguard?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that the beating that he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and he said he thought he was the bodyguard because he did not take part in the questioning. He was there and he was the one who beat him

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could now move on to counts 18 to 20? This is a count that we have discussed in some detail earlier. This is a count involving Elvir Grozdanic observing the accused shove the fire extinguisher hose into the mouth of the man in the wheelbarrow. As you will recall the facts of that incident in brief, on that date Elvir Grozdanic had to perform duties when he was in the hangar building at Omarska. One of the duties that he and the other prisoners had to perform was to clean a portion of the inside of the hangar and then to take the garbage to the garbage container that was located by the kitchen. As he left the hangar to take the garbage to those containers, he saw a group of Serbs, including Dusko Knezevic, in the area of the White House near the hangar entrance. The Serbs had some prisoners there and they were beating and harassing them, making them eat grass like goats. This was not an unusual occurrence at Omarska. You will recall that Hakija Elezovic told you he was made to act like a dog and Emir Beganovic told you a similar story. As the prisoners would be beaten to the point they could no longer respond to the instructions they were given, the prisoners were then put into a wheelbarrow and pushed away by a young Muslim that Elvir knew. Elvir was watching this as he was walking with the garbage toward the containers. As he passed toward the other side of the White House, he saw the accused in a camouflage uniform. The accused had a fire extinguisher in one hand and a hose in the other. He watched as the accused followed the wheelbarrow with the beaten man in it, and saw at a point near the edge of the pista the accused come up to the man and shove the hose of the fire extinguisher into the beaten man's mouth. He does not recall the date of this incident. You will recall from the evidence that he was brought to Omarska on 29th May and he left when the great majority of prisoners were taken away, and we know that date to be 6th August. We have discussed one of the issues in this case, and that deals with the issue of whether this victim was alive or dead at the time this fire hose was shoved into his mouth. There is another issue here, and that has to do with the liability of the accused. You will recall that this victim was being wheeled away after he had been beaten by this group by the White House, and that then when the people could no longer respond they would be put in a wheelbarrow and wheeled away. We suggest that the evidence indicates that the accused was there that day as a part of that group, aiding and abetting that group, giving encouragement to that group and, therefore, this was part of the group activity when he shoved that fire extinguisher into this man's mouth. We cannot forget in determining liability why this beaten man was in the wheelbarrow to begin with. He was in there because of the earlier beatings that had been inflicted upon him by this group of Serbs, including Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Where does that emerge, that this was a regular practice of wheeling away in a wheelbarrow?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The testimony of Elvir Grozdanic, your Honour, was that as these men were beaten to the point they could no longer respond to the orders they were being given, then they were put into wheelbarrows and wheeled away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, the transcript passage I am looking at, it is just that he talks of this particular man being treated in that way.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It must have been assumption on the part of the witness, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As he was coming out, your Honour, he did testify that he saw a man being beaten as he was coming out. He saw the entire thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But the reason why the man was in the wheelbarrow must be an assumption on the part of Grozdanic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We are looking for the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It is page 2798 and 9 -- a very helpful summary. I think you had the witness actually put some stickies on the photograph ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- which demonstrates where everyone was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have those here. We can put these on. What he first said he saw when he first came out was, as he exited the hangar, he saw the group with Knezevic. As you see, as you are looking at the White House to the left in the front of the White House, as he advanced up to about the sidewalk of the White House, then saw the accused on the other side of the White House. As he went further to the garbage containers, ultimately he was near the garbage containers and he saw the accused further up. That was at the point that he saw the accused shove the fire hose into the victim's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, how would you view the fact that in this particular case the witness might have had a grudge against the accused after that confrontation which he had in Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: There was nothing in this evidence, I believe, your Honour, to indicate that the accused saw or recognised Elvir Grozdanic when Elvir Grozdanic saw him. So I do not know that the grudge at that point would be a factor in this description.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I think what Judge Vohrah means is, perhaps, that is a reason for him not to tell the truth. Had he not ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For Elvir Grozdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He had, your Honour. There had been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: The parking incident.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, told him to ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct. You could certainly say that the accused held a grudge against Elvir Grozdanic. You certainly could also think that, perhaps, Elvir Grozdanic held a grudge against the accused. If we go back to his other testimony about seeing the accused in the hangar during the 5 to 11 counts, then I would suggest that that shows he is testifying based on what he saw because he is not the only one who saw the accused there. Again, if he has a grudge and he wants to really get the accused, why does he not do it much more directly? Why does he not say, "I saw him there killing these men". He does not say that. So he is either very subtle in the way he comes across with his grudge, or he was telling you what he saw and what he remembered. The same is true of this incident. Why does he not say, "I saw him up close. I saw him shove this into the man's mouth. I saw the man struggle". He does not come across with facts that would make it easier for you to decide the accused is guilty. He gives you the facts as he remembers them. I think, perhaps, when you look at this count and you ask yourselves, "What other facts would I like to have to make it easy for me to determine that the accused committed the offences?" you will know that this witness did not give you those facts, yet a person with a grudge might very well do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes and then when we return we will continue with this discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Are you leaving 18 to 20?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour. As I had indicated earlier, the evidence proves to you that this was not an isolated, independent act of the accused on this date. He was in the area where these beatings, where making these people act like pigs were occurring. He was present there either to aid and abet in that or to encourage in that or to participate in that himself directly as the victim was taken away and, to add another insult to the victim, he shoves the fire extinguisher hose in the person's mouth. This cannot be said to be mere presence which is such that it alleviates a person of any criminal responsibility, rather, it is significant presence, especially in the light of the other circumstances that we know, the fact that this accused was frequently in Omarska, the conditions of Omarska, the very purpose for which Omarska existed which was to kill, to beat, to torture, non-Serbs which was to be an integral means by which they would achieve the cleansing of opstina Prijedor of non-Serbs. Viewed in that context, we suggest to you that this was not an isolated act and that, therefore, the accused cannot escape culpability by saying, "But all I did was independently on my own stick this fire hose into this man's mouth". We must remember why, if he was dead, he was dead, and it was because of the beating that was inflicted upon him by this group acting against this group of prisoners at Omarska. The accused, of course, does not justify his presence there in any way. He says simply he was never there. If you were to find that the accused's actions during this incident were totally independent of the actions of the group, then the issue becomes whether you can have a violation of Article 5 upon a dead person. In many jurisdictions, of course, alternatively, you could have the possibility of determining if there was an attempt on this accused's part to violate the counts as they are charged, because if, as the evidence would reasonably infer, this accused believed that the victim was alive and he were merely continuing to add to the abuse of this person, then his act would be an attempt to cause serious bodily harm or great suffering, an attempt to commit cruel treatment. Certainly in the condition this person was in in the wheelbarrow, shoving this fire hose in his mouth, even though under other circumstances may not be considered to cause great suffering, certainly under those circumstances it would were the victim alive. Your Honour, Judge Stephen, you have indicated that, according to the evidence, it was Elvir Grozdanic's assumption that this was some sort of practice. Of course, looking at 2799, what Elvir Grozdanic said was that the person had been put in a wheelbarrow, it was a beaten up man, in front of the White House, who could no longer do what they had been asking him to do. So, of course, it would have been an assumption, an inference, on his part from what he saw. There is no direct evidence of people being put in wheelbarrows routinely and taken away, although there is evidence, of course, of unconscious or dead people being taken away to various places in the camp. We suggest that when you look at this evidence in total you will conclude that the accused is guilty of the counts alleged, because he is guilty with the group of what was happening there. In the alternative, we suggest if you determine that in this one instance he did act alone, it was, nonetheless, a violation of Article 5, inhumane acts. Are there any additional questions on 18 to 20?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had one question. On page 2799 of the transcript, line 13, we will go to line 12 first, the question is: "What did you see after that?" This is Mr. Grozdanic talking. Answer: "After that we returned back towards the dormitory and Dusko Tadic -- Dusko Knezevic and Jovic continued to harass, to beat, to ill-treat the inmates who had to grunt as pigs and to pick the grass with their mouth". The way that I read this is the witness testified "Dusko Tadic --", the Court reporter put the dash in there, "Dusko Knezevic. The way that I read that, he made a mistake. He said "Dusko Tadic" and he did not say "I mean Dusko Knezevic", but with the dash and understanding our translation problems, that is how I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I interpret the testimony that was given, what he was saying there at the time is that as he returned back towards the dormitory, Dusko Knezevic and Jovic continued to harass. I do not believe he was intending to say that Dusko Tadic was involved in that activity.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then on page 2800, line 5, the question is: "As you walk toward the containers, you first saw Dule Tadic, is that correct?" Answer: "We first saw Dusko Knezevic and Jovic down there and not far that, as we were moving towards the container, we saw that Muslim and that man driving in a wheelbarrow and an inmate beaten up and Dule Tadic following after them". The way that I read the answer is that "that Muslim" that he refers to is one of the persons who had been beaten by Dusko Knezevic and Jovic when he is talking previously about that incident. Is that the way you read it?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He testified, your Honour, that when he was moving toward the containers he saw a Muslim man whom he recognised. I believe he said the Muslim man's name was Asim (sic), who was actually pushing the wheelbarrow that had the beaten man in it. He saw the accused following behind that. So he saw three people. He saw the man he knew, Asim, pushing the wheelbarrow, the beaten man in the wheelbarrow and the accused following along behind that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How was Asim involved in the previous incident, that is, the one involving Knezevic and Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do not believe he indicates in his evidence anywhere that he saw Asim being beaten, but that Asim was there. When the beaten man could no longer do what he was ordered to do, he saw him put in a wheelbarrow and he saw Asim push him away.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was the beaten man a part of the group that had been beaten, jumped on and forced to act like pigs?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is my understanding of the evidence, your Honour. I believe that is what the evidence indicates, that there was a group of prisoners there by the White House; that this group of Serbs, Dusko Knezevic and the others, were there beating these men; that they beat this man until he could no longer do what he was being ordered to do. Then he was placed in the wheelbarrow. He was pushed away by Asim and, as the witness continued to walk toward the kitchen area where the garbage containers were, then as he approached about at the sidewalk level of the entry into the White House, he saw the accused. Then he saw the accused follow Asim, pushing the wheelbarrow with the beaten man in it. I am sorry the name was Amir. He said Amir was from Prijedor and he thought he was a Muslim, and that was the man pushing the wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again, your Honour, this is further evidence, of course, of using prisoners to take away unconscious or dead people. Many people have testified about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, I wondered if there is anything that you wanted to say in relation to particularly 18 to 20 -- it may apply in other cases -- 18 to 20, we know nothing about the date. The Defence is not only "I was never there", but it is an alibi. Is there anything you want to say about the situation when a defendant raises an alibi and yet the evidence of the offence is not date specific at all.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. What I would say to that is that that fact scenario does not in any way deny the accused a fair trial, because there is nothing in the law that says you can only prosecute crimes where a victim has a date specific as to when the crime occurred. There is nothing in the law that says an accused can say "I am going to raise an alibi defence" in a situation where it is impossible to specify a date. So that a witness who, under the circumstances, cannot give a date does not deny the accused a fair trial. The specificity of the allegations would preclude a second trial on the same charge. That is really, we suggest, where the importance of having a date or time period comes in. They have to be reasonably specific so as to preclude a second charge for the same offence. Here the circumstances put this during the operation of the Omarska camp while this witness was in the camp. We know that he got there 29th May. He left there when most prisoners left, and we know that was 6th August 1992. So it is specific enough that he cannot be tried twice for the same offence. As I said, there is nothing in the law which says you can only try cases where the victim can give a specific date for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The other side of that submission, I suppose, is that if somebody has what he, no doubts, regard as a perfectly good defence by way of alibi, of course, it will be of no real utility if you have a charge which does not have any date at all attached to it other than a period of three months?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, unless the alibi was such that it would show that the accused was not even in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Was in the United States during that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour, yes, but if it is less specific than that, as we would have here with the suggested alibi defence, less specific than that, then, no, it would not address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So that is just misfortune on the part of the accused that the witnesses have not been able to assign a date to the offence?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What I suggest it is, your Honour, is that it is the realities of situations. Again, no accused has the right to raise any specific defence in a case and if the circumstances, the facts, are such that would preclude raising a certain defence for that, that is not unfair to the accused, that is not a denial of fair trial. That is simply these are the facts we have pertaining to this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course, I suppose an alibi defence is one that is really thrust on an accused. If an accused says, "I was never there", then he must have, in effect, an alibi, the two go together?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He could certainly put on alibi evidence that would strengthen his statement "I was never there". He would not be, of course, forced to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But unless the alibi takes him some great distance away, it is not going to be useful because of the absence of a date.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, and then I suggest what you have at that point is what you have without a specific alibi defence, and that is what you are left to do is the task you are about to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is, to evaluate the credibility of these witnesses. One of the factors is what other evidence supports; you do not have to have that in evaluating it. So you are thrust back to an evaluation of the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So really you are saying that the defence in a case such as this has two responses to the charge; first of all, his denial and then a backup to that by way of the alibi ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Or he has ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- and in this particular instance the backup does not avail him but there is still the denial.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He has the denial and then to support that he has the alibi and here that does not support him. We suggest that, looking at the evidence as a whole, this supposed alibi defence does not support him either. But certainly in this instance where there is no specific date, he would not be able to avail himself of that specific alibi evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just with regard to your last statement, it is your position that the alibi does not support his position. That, I guess, is because it is your position that even when the spreadsheets indicate that Mr. Tadic was on duty, that it is your position that he was free and had every ample opportunity to engage in the higher duty, as you have referred to it, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But we certainly could not find as we possibly could find for counts 5 through 11, for example, where the evidence shows that the incident occurred on June 18th and the accused, according to the time sheets, did not go on duty until 9.00 p.m., we could not find for this count that the accused was off duty, could we? How could we find that he was off duty?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For this count?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because there is no date.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What I am saying is that, assuming that he had police duties at the time, those would not avail him of an excuse, an avoidance of criminal liability for the reason we have already, and that is that the police were an integral part of what was going on. If I could use an example from the United States, if we were to have a person who was accused of beating up blacks in the south in the 50s and the person's excuse was, "Well, I could not do that because I had a job at the time", and then the question was ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I wish you would use another example.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- "What kind of a job did you have?" and he said, "Well, I worked for the Ku-Klux-Klan at the time", that would not avail him of an alibi so as to excuse him from criminal liability because, of course, as history shows, the Ku-Klux-Klan was bound up inextricably with mistreating blacks during the 50s. The police in Prijedor were bound up inextricably with the persecution that was going on there. Mr. Prpos's testimony and the other policeman's testimony simply is not credible when they say, "Of course not; people had to be on these traffic checkpoints", even though there was very little traffic, even though there was a curfew, even though there was fuel rationing, "We had to have all these people there, three civilian policemen just to check the civilian vehicles at all times. But, of course, I know nothing about all these other bad things that were going on. So all I can tell you is my people did not get involved in it". I suggest to you that when you look at the overall circumstances here, No. 1, they did know what else was going on; No. 2, they were certainly present when some of these things happened and certainly with Mr. Prpos his traffic policemen were involved in some of that. So it is not true that their checkpoint duties precluded that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just better understand what you are saying? Are you saying that the records that we have seen have been made up in order to provide some defence for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am saying that those records ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Because if they have, of course, they have been a great failure because over and over again they give the wrong dates ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am not saying they have been made up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Then what are you saying? Are you saying that they bothered to fabricate these detailed records to give a cover for other duties?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am saying that what they did was, and what I believe the evidence suggests to you, they used these, they would assign people to checkpoint duties. No doubt, there were times when they were at the checkpoints. I am not saying that at all. What I am saying is that, even though they had those duties, they were free to leave those checkpoints to carry out these other taskings, because they were part of the police who were part of this overall effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I follow that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In regard to whether they were made up or not, I would not suggest that. I say that, however, having made it clear at an earlier time that we were never given the opportunity to even look at these records first-hand to verify where they came out of, what sort of record-keeping was kept. When we took our trip to opstina Prijedor, Mr. Drljaca would not even deign to show us records, let alone let us make copies of them. So we do not know first-hand that they are accurate. It would appear, though, as you say, that certainly I do not think they are made up. I just think they are of no use because I think he could be free to leave to do what he wished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I follow that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The patrol records that relate to the times that the accused is indicated to have served at Orlovci, those are not in evidence, are they? The patrol records for the time, or at least some of them, when he served as a policeman in Kozarac are, because I think one of them was used in cross-examination of Mr. Vujanovic, but there are no patrol records for this time, are there?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, not in evidence. The patrol records that we used, I believe, covered the 1st and 2nd September, I think, the 3rd and 4th or 4th and 5th September and 5th and 6th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Those would have been prepared by the shift supervisor, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe that is correct or they were written out by the people performing the duty and then verified.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before turning to counts 24-28, are there additional questions on 18 to 20? In regard to some of the questions you had asked earlier, Judge McDonald, relating to -- before I get to that, if I could go back to Judge Stephen's questions about Hakija Elezovic and the context in which he said "Keraterm, not in Omarska". Page 2892 of the transcript, I think, gives the question and answer and the exchange so you can see the context better. I believe that actually looking at this he was confused about, "Was this the time Dusko beat me in interrogation?" He says, "That was Keraterm, not Omarska". The questions were basically as follows, starting on line 24 of 2892, and the question was: "Radakovic did not interview you in Omarska; he just happened to be in the ---", and the answer is "No", "-- interrogation centre" follows on. "He was in a first room as you came up the stairs", is the answer. Question: "So you came across this man in the two places, Keraterm and Omarska?" "Yes". "After you had been interviewed, you then went to the White House but were taken around the back of the White House where you have told us you were badly beaten by Dusko. Is that right?" "In Keraterm, it was Dusko who beat me, not in Omarska". I think again the witness is still thinking about the interrogation incident. He was beaten in interrogation at Keraterm. He was not beaten during interrogation at Omarska. It was afterward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then if we can now, Judge McDonald, go back to some of your questions, for example, Ferid Mujcic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I had one question, excuse me, as 18 to 20. Mr. Uzeir Besic testified -- I have not looked recently at the transcript, but he was one of the earlier witnesses -- about seeing Mr. Tadic jump on persons and beat them. Was he referring to 18 to 20?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He was talking about Prijedor, was he?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour, he said that when he was in Omarska camp he was on the pista ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- and a day that he was on the pista, they were sitting looking towards the restaurant building. He heard the noises, the cries, the yells, from what appeared to be behind the restaurant building. Then he looked and he saw the men, he says, who had already come out. So it is not clear if he means out of the restaurant or from around the back of the restaurant. He saw them and the accused, and then everyone on the pista was ordered to lie down. So he lay down on his stomach on the pista. Then, as he was lying there, he heard moans. He looked to the side where the men whom he had seen at the restaurant building were now lying next to him, close to him, on the pista. He looked over there, saw these men lying there, and that is when he saw the accused jumping on these men and beating these men. So it was men lying near him on the pista that he saw.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that is not involved in ... OK. You may go ahead, 24.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do not believe so, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: First of all, I asked you the questions you had asked about 5-11, your Honour. As to Ferid Mujcic, he indicated that he saw the accused. It was when Emir Karabasic was taken out, and he said, "Do you know who it is that took out Emir Karabasic?" This is on pages 1813 to 1815. He is asked, "Do you know who it is that took out Emir Karabasic?" He said, "The guard opened the door and called out his name". "When the door was open, did you look out of the door?" "Yes". "When you looked out of the door, what did you see?" "I looked through the door and I saw Dusko Tadic standing behind the guard, and with him another, slightly taller. They were standing about a metre-and-a-half to two behind the guard". So he indicates it was the guard, your Honour. Muharem Besic ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- indicates that in response to a question, "The door was opened when Jasko finally left the room?" "Yes, exactly. Jasko opened the door. At the very door there was a lot of people right around the door", and he is talking, your Honour, about inside the door. "They were almost on top of each other so that you could not just go straight to the door. You had to walk and avoid people's feet or hands or heads". "Do you know how long the door remained open after Jasko left?" "When Jasko went out, you could see Dule clearly, and as he", meaning Jasko, "was stepping over the doorstep, Dule cursed his mother and you could hear a blow". When he talks about hearing someone called out, he says he heard the name and then he looked up and he saw that Dule Tadic was there. He said he thought he recognised the voice as Dule Tadic's, but he told you that he did not see the person as the name was being called out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are saying he did not see the person while they were being called out, but did after the door was opened?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. He also said that he did not actually see a blow delivered; he heard a blow after Jasko went out.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And Velic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Emsud Velic ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What page of the transcript was Besic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was 2683, 2684. When Velic is talking, Velic says on pages 3421 at line 22, when he is asked in part "Did you recognise the guard that came to the door first of all?" "No". "You told us that it was the guard who opened the door first of all". "Yes". "Did the guard come into the room?" "No". Then on 3423 he is being cross-examined, he said, "You spent longer looking at the ground ---" He said, "I do not think so". The end of the question was, "-- than you did at the door?" He says, "I do not think so. I did not know. I spent much time looking at the door than to the ground".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not inconsistent, Velic and Besic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: One sees Mr. Tadic, one sees a guard, open the door?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, because he sees that it was the guard who opened the door, he said. He said that he saw a guard at the door. It was a guard who came to the door, opened the door. That is what got his attention when the door opened. Then he says that he looks to the door, he sees the guard at the door and he sees Tadic. This was the first time that Jasko was called out, the time that he did not respond. Then the second time that Jasko was called out when he did respond, Velic told you at that time "I thought I saw him, but I am not 100 per cent sure", "him" meaning "I thought I saw the accused again at the door but I am not 100 per cent sure".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then Besic then is talking about the second time that he was called out?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He is talking about the time when Hrnic actually goes out of the door.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And sees the accused?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In regard to Emsud Velic on that point, on 3410 he begins to say on line 2: "While the door was opening and there was one of the guards opening the door", and while he was opening the door then Jasko was going to the door. I am sorry. "As the guard opened the door, the guard was going with the door, leaning on the door", and then he says that he saw the guard and he saw Dusko Tadic in the doorway. You will recall that Emsud Velic told you that he saw Tadic looking at people, looking around at the people in the room, but he also says that it was a guard there at the door that he saw as well as Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about Kenjar and Grozdanic in terms of the calling out?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, before that, I do have for Armin Mujcic again on pages 2762 and 2763, Armin Mujcic indicates that he is, as I said, sitting on this bench or table, low table, near room A15. He looks over and he sees the accused and the group coming from the direction of the WC. He does not in his testimony say that he actually saw them come in the door into the hangar. He would not have been able to see that from where he was. So he hears "The mottled ones are here". He then hurries to try to get into the room. He looks back and he sees the accused and this group coming in the direction of the WC. In relation to Kenjar, what was your specific question about him, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What was his testimony regarding the calling out of persons?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On page 2565 he begins that and he indicates that he heard the name Jasko Hrnic called and he said first he was called out Asko Hrnic. We understood that they were calling out Asko Hrnic at that point. Then he is asked about Enver Alic and he goes on. Down on line 32 on the page it says, "When Jasko Hrnic was called out as Asko, did he go out right away? Did he respond?" "No". Then on 2566, the question is asked, "Was he called out more than once?" "Yes, yes. We heard Jasko Hrnic being called out, but I cannot remember. Perhaps it was several times. We heard it once at that place where we were". "Did Jasko finally respond or say anything to the calling out of his name?" "Only when the door opened, Jasko said 'There is Jasmin Hrnic here, there is no Asko'. Then the individual who was in the doorway in front of the door said, 'It is you we need'." Then he says, "From that position, were you able to see the door?" Armin Kenjar says, "No", from his position he could not see the door. So he is telling you what he heard. Elvir Grozdanic, as you recall, was in the WC. He had been taken there by his Serb friend, the guard at Omarska, and was hiding there. When he came out, as he went to his room, that was when he saw Jasko Hrnic. He did not indicate he heard any of the people being called out from his hiding place in the WC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: While you are dealing with counts 5 to 11, I am missing page 36 of your very useful excerpts from the transcript dealing with 5 to 11.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We will rectify that right now, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can you? Thank you very much.
