utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I apologise for that. Your Honour, Judge McDonald, do you have any additional ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did Ferid Mujcic identify the accused as being called out?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did Ferid Mujcic identify the accused as being called out?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The accused as being called out?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry. Did he identify the accused as calling out Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did not indicate that. He said that the guard called him out. Are there any additional questions on 5 to 11?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any evidence that anyone saw Mr. Alic being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not believe that we have -- we do have evidence, I believe, from -- just a moment, your Honour. Your Honour, Armin Mujcic indicated that he saw Eno Alic and the others being beaten. You recall he said he had finally gotten into A15. He was up on the landing. He said he saw them beaten and it was by a group of Serbs. He said he thought it was the group that the accused had come in with. He did not identify the accused as being there with them when that beating he observed was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any conflict, as you see it, or inconsistency between Ferid Mujcic's testimony regarding the calling out of Karabasic and Hodzic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Yes, your Honour. There is certainly a contradiction in that Ferid Mujcic says that Emir Karabasic is called out of room A17. Husein Hodzic says that Emir Karabasic is called out of the room upstairs, B14. I believe that that confusion is explained by the fact that Emir Karabasic visited with Jasko Hrnic in that room and that, in his recollection of those events, Mr. Mujcic confused an occasion when he was in the room with that occasion when he heard the name Armin Karabasic called out, because Emir Mujcic then does tell you that he also heard and saw when Jasko Hrnic was called out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And they were not in the same room?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: They were not in the same room. Jasko Hrnic in A17 and Emir Karabasic was upstairs in that big room, through the stairwell room, up in B14 upstairs.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So he could not have seen both of them called out of the same room?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you say it can be explained by the fact that Karabasic visited the room?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because I think, your Honour, in his recollection he is confused about seeing Emir Karabasic in that room. Jasko Hrnic was in the room. He had been very badly beaten. He used that table as his resting place. In Ferid Mujcic's testimony, he said Emir Karabasic was there in the room up on the table sitting there with Jasko Hrnic. No doubt, when Emir Karabasic would come to visit Jasko in that room, he would sit up there on that table. So I believe it was his seeing him there on earlier occasions that led to his confusion about that day.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you hear persons being called out from the upper room? As I recall ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It was very open.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- there was testimony that persons would come to the bottom floor, I thought, and call out.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: They called out and also because of the openness of the upstairs, you were able to hear people called out. You recall that people in room 15 told you they heard people called out. Again this was a very open repair type facility with some offices upstairs, but with this huge hangar area. Offices had windows on to the hangar area, and you were able to hear from there. People did testify that they did hear people being called out. You are correct for room A15, for that entire huge area which comprised A15 on the ground floor, the stairwell going on up and the corridor upstairs and B14, the guards did not go up there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So could Mr. Mujcic have heard Mr. Karabasic being called out?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the ground floor in A17. He certainly could have heard that. Again you are correct that the guards did not go upstairs into that big room. It was too crowded. They probably even in that setting would have felt somewhat insecure trying to push their way through all those prisoners to go upstairs. So for the A15 area, they went there and called out and then people heard that upstairs as well as it was relayed upstairs.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So he could have heard him being called out but could not have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for this next portion of the argument at some point I am going to ask that we go into closed session because of the nature of the testimony one of the witnesses gave in closed session. I do not know if it is going to take a few minutes to do that or not? Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How long do you expect it will take you to present your closing for counts 24 to 28?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This is 24 through 28 and then 29 through 34.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You need a closed session for both or just 24 to 28?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, just a portion of 24-28.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: How long do you think you will need then for the 24-28?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For the closed?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought that you would just need a portion of the time for closed ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I just say just to the Court simply to switch off the sound so we can proceed without having the curtains down?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If both the sound and the feed from the overhead projector is switched off, of course, we have no objection to that. Again, if we are talking about perhaps, depending on questions, five to 10 minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It will be before lunch in any case. That is a good suggestion then. Do you have any objection to proceeding without the sound, and you were going to use the Elmo?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have extra copies of what you were going to use? Is that what would be necessary?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We do have extra copies and then perhaps we would not have to use the Elmo either.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any objection to hearing this portion of the closing statement in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you need to tell us when you want to go into closed. Now?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. You give us the sign and then the technician will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, turning now to counts 24 to 28, these counts charge the accused with the killing of four men at the Kalate junction in Kozarac on 27th May 1992. The evidence was presented by three witnesses and the evidence proves the crimes charged. The men taken out that day have never been seen since that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me one minute. We will give the sign when we need to go into closed. We are in open now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The men taken out that day have never been seen since that time. The evidence proves, in addition to the fact that these men are dead, that the accused is the one who committed the killings. On 27th May, you recall the testimony that a very long and very large column of Muslims was surrendering from various locations in the Kozarac area, including Brdjani and Vidovici. In that column were Salko Karabasic and his son, Sejdo, Sulejman Besic and Ferid Mujcic. Salko Karabasic, Sulejman Basic and Ferid Mujcic were in different places in that column. Your Honour, as you had mentioned earlier, witness U testified that on that date he was also in that column, but you will recall also that he testified that he was at the head of the column and that he actually reached the intersection of the main road at 8.30 or 9 o'clock in the morning. This incident occurred in the afternoon. So he was certainly in the very forefront of that column, this very, very long column. He would not have been in a position to see this incident. As the column made its way from Brdjani toward the Mutnik mosque, armed Serb soldiers were on the sides of the road and there was a tank there as well. When the column reached the intersection with the Marsala Tita Street at the Mutnik Mosque, a Serb soldier directed the column to go left and go down Marsala Tita Street toward the new Prijedor/Banja Luka highway intersection. People were sent on from there to separation points where men and boys aged 15 and over were separated from women and children. The column was indeed very long, and sometimes spread out in spots, sometimes more bunched up and in other areas very spread out. As the portion of the column Salko, Sulejman and Ferid was in came towards the Kalate intersection, each of them saw a part of a crime that was committed there. All three men passed by the location of the two kiosks on the corner of Marsala Tita at the Kalate junction. The kiosk faced on to Marsala Tita Street. Before they passed there, or as they were passing, all three men saw Muslim policemen lined up against the kiosk there, at least some of whom they all knew. All three men saw the accused whom they knew there with Goran Borovnica whom they also knew. All three men saw the accused and Borovnica armed. As Salko Karabasic approached the intersection, he saw the accused and Goran Borovnica there. If you will look at the overhead, we have here a copy of the diagram that he created for you during his testimony. You see that he marks where the column was. On there he marks where he saw the accused and where he saw Borovnica as he approached that intersection. He told you that as he approached that intersection, he saw his brother Ismet and Redzep Foric had already been singled out of the column and were already at that chicken kiosk. Then he saw the accused ordering Goran Borovnica to take certain men from the column. Those men included Salko's brother Ekrem and then his son Sejdo and a man that Salko Karabasic referred to as Meho Mujkan. As the accused would order it, Borovnica would do it. Then at that point Salko was forced to go on with the column and he saw nothing of what had happened after that. Ferid Mujcic also saw the accused at that junction and he also saw Goran Borovnica at that junction. Again if you will look at the overhead, you will see the diagram that Ferid Mujcic created for you showing where he saw these people. You will recall that he told you he saw the accused there standing behind Goran Borovnica. Goran Borovnica was standing behind the men who had already been called out and men who had already been placed up against the chicken kiosk. The men that he recognised who were placed up against the chicken kiosk were Ismet Karabasic, Ekrem Karabasic, Sejdo Karabasic, Redzep Foric and a fifth person about whose identity he was uncertain, telling you that perhaps it was Fikret Alic but he was uncertain about that. He testified that he saw Goran Borovnica strike one of the policeman, Ekrem Karabasic. He testified that he saw Sejdo Karabasic, Redzep Foric and this fifth man about whose identity he is uncertain being taken across the front of the column to the other side of the street. Then his portion of the column was again forced to walk faster and he moved on. At this point, your Honour, we will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will go into private session at this time. The sound will be turned off as well as the connection to the Elmo.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are now in public session. Go ahead. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Turning now to counts 29 to 34, you recall these are the counts that arise from the rounding up, beating and killing of the men ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you need to go into private session on any of these? Did we not receive some names on sheets of paper?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour. Your Honour, I am going to refer to that exhibit and the letters that were indicated on that exhibit and that was Prosecution Exhibit 285. There were letters for people who were killed and there were numbers for people who were beaten and taken away. Your Honours, you will recall that the evidence of this incident is that on 14th June 1992 the accused and other Serbs were involved in the rounding up and taking away of Muslim men in the village of Sivci and the hamlet of Jaskici. You will recall from the testimony that Jaskici can be reached from Sivci by following a track that runs through the woods and forest, and it can be reached if you are walking in about 10 minutes. So the hamlet is basically behind Sivci. The evidence here proves the counts beyond reasonable doubt. As far as for the murders, the witnesses from Jaskici established that the victims A through E are dead. They also established that victims 1 through 14 were viciously beaten, some of them passing out from the beatings and then taken away never to be seen again, except for one man, Salih Softic, who was later seen in Trnopolje camp. Six witnesses testified. Five of them testified that the accused was the one who committed the alleged offences. One of the six did not know the accused. Four of the five who said that the accused committed the offences knew the accused from before. The fifth person, Zemka Sahbaz, recognised the accused when shown a photographic lineup. All of these witnesses had the opportunity to see the accused from a close distance during the day. One of the witnesses reacted with relief when she saw the accused there, thinking that since he knew her he must know some of the men in that hamlet, so that perhaps the killings and other mistreatment would not occur. The evidence in the case proves that her relief was unwarranted. On 14th June 1992 when the accused and these other Serbs carried out this roundup they began in Sivci. At about 1.00 p.m. on that day Serb soldiers came to the home of Sakib Sivac who lived in Sivci and took him from his home. They took him and other Muslim males to another Muslim home in the village, making them run, lie down, run again, lie down all the way. They beat the men as they ran. Some of them were beaten quite badly. When they arrived at a particular house they were kept there in the yard until buses came, and then they were loaded on to buses. Sakib Sivac got on to the rear door of the last bus. He told you that as he was moving in this column toward the buses the column was moving very slowly. He told you that people were keeping their heads down trying not to look so as to invite further abuse. He was keeping his head down, but when the column slowed down he looked up to see what was going with the column. He told you at that time he recognised the accused and another person that Sakib Sivac knew, a person by the name of Cavic. He saw the two of them. He recognised the two of them and then he continued moving on to get on to the bus. He told you that he knew Cavic better than he knew the accused, that he had socialised with Cavic, and that he continued to look at Cavic, he told you possibly thinking that Cavic could help him. He continued to look at him and his continued looking at Cavic resulted in a push which moved him onward. When he got the push he turned in the direction of the push. At that moment he saw the accused wearing a camouflage uniform and carrying an automatic weapon. So he saw them as he came up, and then as he went past them he got the push and he turned and saw the accused standing face to face, just a rifle's length away from him. He also told you that he got on to the bus then. He got on to the bottom step. He was facing outward through the glass doors. He was able to see the accused and look at him then as the bus was there, and then began slowly to move away. He testified to you that he was taken from that village to Keraterm camp. Later that afternoon before 3.00 p.m. the accused and other Serbs left Sivci and went to Jaskici, a hamlet of Muslim families and one Catholic family. The Serbs went down that path that runs between Sivci and Jaskici. The people in Jaskici that day were in their homes, Sunday afternoon. When the accused and the others got to the homes of Abaz and Nijaz Jaskici, the houses near Sivci, the inference from the evidence is that they called these men out as well. The two men there, Abaz and Nijaz, were shot in the field behind the home of Ilijaz Elkasovic. Sena Elkasovic told you when she looked out the window she saw these men back in what she called her vegetable garden area. Several of the people in Jaskici first knew the Serbs were coming and were there when they heard loud gunfire close at hand. That was Sena and Senija who told you that. The evidence also suggests that at that time the Serbs separated, some Serbs going to Abaz and Nijaz, going to the bodies, and the accused and others going on down the path to Jaskici. The accused and one other went to the home of Huso Jaskic and called out his son, Ismet Jaskic, and a relative who was there, Hasan Jakupovic, one of the many refugees who was that day in the village of Jaskici, having been driven from their homes in other areas of the opstina. While the accused was doing that, was bringing out Ismet and Hasan, other Serbs went to the home of Salko Jaskic and Draguna Jaskic and called all the people there out, men and women included. When the people came out the men were placed over by the garage or barn area, and the women and children were put by the house steps. One of the soldiers in Draguna's house fired in the house. While the people were outside the house Draguna saw the accused bringing Ismet and Hasan from Huso's house toward hers. For your assistance we have prepared a demonstrative aid based on her testimony to show you where it is she said she first saw the accused as she stood outside her house. As you look at the photo you can see at the very left corner what appears to be the very bottom of her steps. She told you that the women and children were there at that position, and that when she saw the accused he was back over in the area where this X is. He was coming down the road from Huso's house toward her. She testified to you that when she first saw him with Ismet and with Hasan, that she saw that he was coming along behind Ismet, he was beating Ismet and that Ismet was bloody. She told you that when she first saw the accused he was some 20 metres away from her, and that when he finally came to a stop in this area where we have the circle that is straight across from the white portion of the house across the road, that the accused was about 10 metres away from her at that point. With her that day was her sister Subha Mujic who also testified here. She was outside that day. She also saw the accused coming down the road with Ismet and with Hasan. Both Draguna Jaskic and her sister had known the accused in passing for many years, and both told you that they recognised him. There was shooting, very loud and direct shooting, and that shooting brought out Zemka Sahbaz who was another refugee who had originally come from Jaskici and then when she married moved away. She was now back in Jaskici because it was no longer safe for her to be in her home. On that date she was in the home of Ahmet Jaskic, the house that was directly across the street from the home of Salko Jaskic and Draguna Jaskic. She told you that on that date, hearing this loud gunfire, this din and then very loud fire, very close, she came out of her yard to see what caused that and she saw the accused, the man she later identified as the accused, and another soldier bringing Ismet and Hasan down the road. You will recall that she told you that she basically saw them when they were near this shrub that is marked here at the very end of the line of hedges there. That is when she saw them. When she first saw the accused she told you that he was looking toward Draguna Jaskic's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is the house from which the photograph is taken?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it is. She said that she saw the men and the women out in the yard at Draguna Jaskic's house, and that the accused was looking in that direction. She went on to tell you that at some point then the accused noticed her and turned toward her and ordered her back into Ahmet's house, telling her to bring out the other people that were in that house. She then went back, as she was ordered, into Ahmet's house. At this time Draguna and the others also went back into Draguna's house, that is Draguna and the other women and children. As they entered the house Draguna and her sister, Subha, saw the men from her house taken to the road and beaten when they got there. So as they were going into the house they were able to see the men led out to the street and they were able to see them being beaten as they were led out to the street. Then they entered the house. They had been ordered to lie on the floor in the house, but Draguna and her sister could not do so because of what they feared was happening to their husbands, their relatives. So instead of going in and lying down on the floor, they went into the room. If you will look at the overhead we have the picture looking out the window of the view they would have had that day. They went into a room and instead of lying down, they went to the window and they looked for a time to see what was happening. When they were in that room looking out the window, what they saw was the accused about 12 metres away beating the men who were lying on the road. Subha Mujic told you that when Draguna saw what was happening there she said: "Look how Dule is beating our family." Her sister Subha who was also seeing this replied: "Yes." They also saw water thrown on the men when they passed out, water taken from Draguna's well. They saw their father tried to rise and the accused strike him down again, then Draguna's son made her lay back down on the floor. At this time the other Serbs who had split off and gone to the bodies of Abaz and Nijaz continued their way to Senija Elkasovic's house and there they came into the house and they ordered the men of the house out of the house. At this time we suggest to you that what the evidence shows is that the accused then moved from his position on the road to the next house over, that was Senija Elkasovic's house, to stand there and supervise as the men from that house were brought out. Senija Elkasovic looked out the window as the men from her house were taken out, and she saw the accused there in her yard in the place that is marked on this photograph, this demonstrative aid. Again this is a demonstrative aid, we are marking this from the transcript. It is not an exhibit which the witness marked. She saw the accused standing in this area and she saw him there looking toward her house waiting for the men to come out. She recognised the accused. She saw the men from her house come out and pass. It appears from her testimony that when they passed they passed through what would have been the left side of the accused as you see him there. He comes out, they pass to the left and then the accused, we suggest, then followed them back. What Senija Elkasovic told you was as she saw them pass she then was ordered by a soldier in her house to lie down on the floor. She just got this one look as she saw the men coming out and walking past the accused. The accused at this time went back to the men who were lying on the road between the houses of Draguna and Ahmed Jaskic and stood on the side of the road nearest Ahmet's house. At this time Zemka and the others came out of Ahmet's house. She told you that she came out first. They came out in a line, she was in front, and when she came out for the entire time she was out there she watched the accused. She told you she watched him because he appeared to be the one who was in charge there giving the orders. She indicated to you that she saw the accused nod to another soldier, a blond soldier, and then that soldier began to beat the men lying on the road, village men and refugees whose names she did not know. Then she and the others were ordered back into the house, and ordered to go back into the house one at a time. As she went in with her young son Jasmin, he was called out by the accused. He was called to "come here". As her son went toward the accused she followed him as she got near to the gate, and at that time the accused came and she said he kicked on the fence and said to her, "Bula, you have come to recognise someone?" At that point in time her daughters came and took her back into the house. After the men were taken from Senija's house and she and her family were lying on the floor at some point Senija told you she heard, "Don't raise your head", then shots. Her mother got up and looked out the window and said: "They are killing them." We suggest to you that the evidence proves it was at this time that the bodies seen on the road near Sead Elkasovic's house, it was at this time that these men were killed. When the mother stood up and looked out the window and said, "They are killing them", the Serb soldier who was in the house with them forced her mother to get back down on to the floor. After a time Senija looked outside her house and saw the men being taken away down the road in the direction of Kozarac. At Draguna's house, Draguna and Subha also got up once again, and when they got up they saw the accused beating Jasmin and taking the men down from the village down the road in the direction of Kozarac. When all was quiet the women went and found the five dead bodies they identified for you on Exhibit 285. The women also identified for you 14 men who were taken away that day, husbands, fathers, brothers, relatives, sons. These men have never been heard from again, except for the one man, Salih Softic, who was seen at Trnopolje camp. After this occasion there were only three elderly men left in that village, the others were dead or missing. Some left the hamlet immediately that day to Trnopolje. Sena Jaskic told you she went to a place called Kararici where later she was forced to leave. Soldiers came and forced her to go to Trnopolje, to the camp there. Others such as Senija Elkasovic remained in the hamlet for a time, but were eventually also forced to leave. Senija told you that they were also forced to go to Trnopolje camp, to get permission to bury the dead men and that eventually they got that permission and they took them to Sivci and they buried them in a common grave in Sivci. After the men were killed or taken away, Senija Elkasovic told you that in the following days Serbs came to the village and took away everything, saying such things as "This is our place, not your's. You are going to Turkey. You are leaving anyway. You won't need this tractor, this car". Serbs from all over came and took away the possessions of the families whose home had been Jaskici until there were no more inhabitants left there. Five witnesses told you about the crimes this accused committed in Sivci and Jaskici on 14th June 1992. They all saw them clearly and from nearby. Four of the five knew him from before and Zemka Sahbaz picked him out of a photo lineup. There has been some emphasis and certainly some questions in cross-examination in this trial concerning the showing of a photographic lineup book to Draguna Jaskic, the woman who was so frightened for her family that you recall up until the last minute she was going to be given protective measures. The Prosecution brought out the facts surrounding that lineup and her reaction. Dr. Wagenaar in his testimony told you, "Well, a reaction like that, we do not know what it is. It should not be called an identification. It should be brought to the court's attention". That is what was done. It was also brought to the Defence's attention. They had that information before the witness testified. What do we make of the information concerning Draguna Jaskic's viewing of the photospread identification? You will recall that when she was shown that book, at the end of it she was asked if she recognised anyone in that book and she said "No". She did not equivocate. She said "No". You will recall also that while she was viewing the book, contrary to her later "no", when she came upon the photograph of the accused there was an immediate intense reaction. I suggest it was a reaction that all of us equate to a reaction of recognition. What was the reaction? The reaction was an immediate, drastic reaction. The eyes widened. She moved back and forth. There was an expulsion of breath. All of that is consistent with what, in our human experience? It is consistent with a person seeing something that evokes an anxiety, a fearful response. Why would this witness see the accused and have a such a frightened response evoked? Because it was the accused who, in effect, ended her life as she knew it on 14th June in the hamlet of Jaskici. That is not a reaction that lacks understanding. Dr. Wagenaar told you that the first reaction, the first indication, to be recognition or not recognition, that is what is decisive. That is that happened here. It was not a verbal response, but it was a human, physical reaction we are all familiar with, and that reaction said, "That is the man that I am afraid of. That is the man that I have reason to fear". That was a recognition. You have the evidence before you. You have the explanation. You must evaluate that. But we suggest to you that when you evaluate it, you will determine that, in fact, this was a fearful reaction to a man she recognised as the man who committed the crimes in Jaskici on 14th June 1992. Zemka Sahbaz was shown a photo lineup and she also picked the accused. In her testimony, like the others who had been shown photo lineups, she was asked whether she watched television, whether she had media exposure. She told you in the country she was she did not have a satellite dish. That country did not really carry those programmes. She told you, "My husband was in three camps. We do not watch television. We do not watch violence. If I want to watch something, it is not violence. I do not want to be reminded of what happened there". Some people may be sceptical of that response, but again, based on your knowledge of human nature, it is a human response to a catastrophe that has changed their lives, changed their lives irrevocably. That is an understandable explanation. That is a credible explanation. There is no direct evidence in this case that the accused shot and killed the men who were murdered in Jaskici on that date, but he is, nonetheless, guilty of those murders. He was acting in concert with these others on that date. He was participating in this rounding up of the Muslims in that village. This was a single transaction. Parts of it were killing them, parts of them were beating them, parts of it were taking them away. There is no evidence at all to indicate any type of affirmative or decisive removal of himself from this ongoing activity so as to alleviate him of responsibility for those deaths. He is guilty of the murders as well as of the beatings that occurred there in that hamlet on that day. There has been some discussion before we began this trial about the issue of intent when it comes to wilful killing or murder. We suggest to you that in these counts, as well in the other counts alleging murder, the issue of intent that was raised before the trial began is not an issue here, because that issue was if the evidence were to show a person had the intent to commit serious bodily harm, and the facts show that the victim died, would that intent to cause serious bodily harm of itself be sufficient to sustain a murder conviction? These facts that you have before you in each one of these scenarios where the accused participated in murders, the intent shows, the intent to kill, either a premeditated intent or the intent to kill that can be inferred from the fact that we assume a person intends the natural and probable consequences of their act. So the issue concerning intent only to do serious bodily harm, we suggest, is not raised by this evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying then that the accused must have had a homicidal intent, which is the position of the Defence? I do not think that is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am saying I do not think the issue arises under these facts.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying then -- why?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because I believe that, looking at the evidence before you, the only reasonable conclusion to draw from that evidence is that either, No. 1, there was a premeditated intent, if you will, or No. 2, that there is intent under what some jurisdictions would call second degree murder or unpremeditated murder, in that the acts that occurred that day were acts of which the natural and probable consequence was the death of the victims, so that the intent to kill can be inferred from that. There is no indication at all that the only thing that could possibly have happened here was serious injury to these victims, not in the light of all circumstances that we know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So the intent then, you would say, that you have shown is an intent to commit more than a serious injury?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We believe the facts show that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for lunch until 2.30. I was wondering whether you were completed, but you will complete when we return.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I can hear you without seeing you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence the Prosecution has presented to you in this case meets the burden of proof required. The Defence evidence does not introduce reasonable doubt. The accused testified in these proceedings. His testimony is not credible. He, of course, has the most obvious reason to be untruthful and he has been. Of course, he had full knowledge of what the Prosecution and Defence witnesses had said when he testified. He could match his testimony to the story he thought best suited his needs. The Defence also called the accused's wife, his brother, his sister-in-law and a witness who is the accused's wife's cousin. Those relationships of themselves do not mean the witnesses are unbelievable, but the relationships must be considered in evaluating credibility. I have discussed the relative significance of the work schedules, the police work schedules, both the degree to which they can be relied upon as accurate and the relative likelihood that, even if accurate, they disclose the accused's whereabouts or actual duties at any particular time. Even if the accused worked for an organisation which maintained records of unimpeachable accuracy (which is not true), or even if he had worked for an organisation which was not itself an integral part of the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor, rather than the opposite, these records would have little impact on this case because the times listed simply do not preclude his commission of the crimes in this case. He may have had a job but his work with the police did not prevent him from committing these crimes. The accused has, however, presented to you an additional argument. He has painted himself as the type of person who would never become involved in inter-ethnic conflict. At page 6062 of the transcript the accused includes himself in "We, simple, ordinary people did not know much about things at that time". He has attempted to convince the Court that he was a simple, ordinary man, a common man without any interest or involvement in politics, someone who did not even know, according to his testimony, whether the Serbian authorities in opstina Prijedor intended the creation of Republika Srpska. In short, the accused has painted himself as the last person to be involved in crimes such as the ones charged. His attempt to paint himself in this manner in the face of compelling evidence to the contrary reveals to you both his willingness to lie to this Court and his awareness of the implications of that evidence. Was the accused, indeed, a simple, ordinary person with no involvement in national politics? To answer that, you need look no further than the work report, the report he prepared about his work on behalf of the SDS. That answers that question. The man who did not know whether the SDS was interested in the creation of Republika Srpska emphasised to those same authorities in his report his credentials as "an earnest SDS member and enthusiastic supporter of the idea of creating Republika Srpska". In the report he complained about his treatment by Prijedor authorities, "After all I had done since 1990, only wishing to contribute to the creation of our common country even when it implied risking my life and my family's safety". His activities to achieve that goal included joining forces with fellow SDS activist, Milos Radulovic, and trying to organise assignments to be implemented which, as arranged, were to come into effect should fighting start, trying to persuade Serbs not to serve on sentry post duties with non-Serbs; repeatedly attempting to obtain information about the number and nature of weapons that may exist in the Kozarac reserve police; working with Vaso Radonjic, the secretary, and resignation of the shoe factory, in trying to get weapons which were stored at the Prijedor barracks. This is not even a simple ordinary SDS member, much less a simple, ordinary, uninvolved, common man. In his efforts to falsely depict himself as a simple man uninvolved in SDS activities, the accused has attempted to falsely characterise the plebiscite. He told this Court that the plebiscite was not conducted at the behest of the Serbian authorities, but on behalf of the entire opstina at the behest of the local Municipal Assembly, despite the fact the document which appointed him is stamped on it by the SDS and is headed "Plebiscite of Serb people". He also said this despite the fact that the plebiscite ballot (which is Exhibit 97) shows that it was conducted by the "Assembly of the Serbian people". He says this, despite the fact that he boasts in his work report of having been "entrusted" with the task of conducting the plebiscite by the main board of the SDS. Of course, Judge Stephen, you are correct when you say that the accused's responsibilities were local. It is also true, however, that the plebiscite was extremely important to the Serb leadership because it was this plebiscite that served as the basis for the declaration of a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and responsibility for conducting the plebiscite, as you heard from witness P, was greater in a predominantly non-Serb area such as Kozarac. More to the point, the significance of the plebiscite can be gauged by the accused's false characterisation of its nature and source. We can also appreciate its significance to the Serbs by noting that the accused is able to denounce Serbs in his work report for failing to vote in that plebiscite. Such efforts at masking the accused's true character and activities are not limited to the accused himself. Mira Tadic and Ljubo Tadic were, of course, well aware of the accused's views and activism, but they also painted him as a completely uninterested man who had no interest in politics or nationalism. In considering their testimony, however, we ask you to remember that Mira Tadic was an SDS member who, with her husband, organised that plebiscite. We also ask you to remember that Ljubo Tadic was an SDS member who railed against the jihad, the holy war, that Muslims had allegedly launched against all Christians, not just orthodox, and which supposedly justified the destruction of Kozarac. The blatant attempt of all three to match their stories to provide the accused a defence is seen in areas other than in support of his alleged political non-involvement. For example, regarding his mobilization. In his record of interview, the accused described his mobilization as follows, that he was in Banja Luka on 15th June and he discusses in detail the people he saw and was with on that date. He tells you that on 16th June he travelled to Prijedor with his brother Ljubo. He saw police officials and was accepted into the traffic police. He was told he was free to leave and did not report for duty that day. As he was leaving, he was given his military book in which that day, June 16th 1992, had been recorded. He and Ljubo spent some time at a cafe called Aero Club with an acquaintance ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is this his evidence or ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This is from his oral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- a prior statement?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This is from his ICTY record of interview. He tells you that he and Ljubo spent time at this club, this cafe, Aero Club, and that Ljubo left about 1 o'clock. He then went on to name the people he saw during the rest of the day. He told you that he spent that night in the home of Radovan and Dusanka Vokic. In that oral lie, he tells you that the next day, the 17th, he went to the police station in the morning with Vokic and he was on duty at Orlovci for the first time that day, the 17th. After he finished at the checkpoint, he indicated that he went to Pecani; discusses who he was with and again indicated that he spent the night at the home of Radovan Vokic. In that oral lie, he said that the next day, the 18th, he stayed around Prijedor and he names the people he was allegedly with. Mira Tadic was not one of the people he included as seeing or being with that day. The accused described these events as related both in May and then again in December in those records of interview. He related the events in great detail and volunteered that he remembered very well the dates and events. But then at this trial Mira Tadic came to testify and her version was quite different. According to her, the accused left Banja Luka for Prijedor by himself, not with Ljubo, on 15th June. He came back to Banja Luka the next evening wearing a police uniform. He spent the night in Banja Luka, not in Prijedor at the Vokic home as he said in his record of interview. She testified that the two of them went to Prijedor together the next day, the 17th, and that night they spent at the home of Martin and Mileva Dzaja, not in the Vokic home alone as the accused indicated in his record of interview. She testified she left some time the next day for Banja Luka. Then when the accused testified, having of course heard his wife's testimony, he changed from his story in the oral lie and he told you his wife's story. Now it was his version that he left Banja Luka on Monday 15th by himself; that he talked with police officials on that day; that his first day at Orlovci was 16th; that he returned to Banja Luka to fetch Mira and spent the night with her at the home of Martin and Mileva Dzaja on the second night of his duty which would be the 17th. In short, having heard her testimony he gave the same story. When asked on cross-examination about this revision, the accused accused Mr. Reid, saying that Mr. Reid had insisted on the dates. But when asked if Mr. Reid had also insisted that the accused tell him on more than one occasion "I remember very well", the accused said maybe he did not insist that much. In fact, it was the accused in these interviews who insisted to Mr. Reid that Mr. Reid provide dates for allegations. Then it was the accused who responded with specific information about his alleged whereabouts on those dates. Now, when this excuse failed, instead of blaming Mr. Reid, the accused tried to excuse the change in his version by saying that he knew that there would ultimately be documents with the exact dates. Again this excuse was false. In fact, the accused had with him in December documents which listed the exact dates. When pressed about this, the accused admitted it, but said, "I just skimmed it and did not pay much attention to the details". Again this was another example of the accused's dissembling. In fact, he did use those documents in formulating his answers. No example could be clearer than this. He stated to Mr. Reid that he was not on duty on July 20th 1992 and was in the centre of town. At that time his lawyer pointed out the document with the dates on it to Mr. Tadic and showed it to Mr. Reid. The accused then stated that on 20th July he was on duty in Orlovci from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m.. The cites of the references that I have just made, your Honours, is in the December record of interview, pages 41 and 42. These were lies to cover an earlier lie to cover an even earlier lie and, ultimately, to cover the biggest lie of all, that the accused was not involved in these events in opstina Prijedor as charged in the indictment. As I indicated, this attempt to conform their stories appears throughout the testimony of the Tadic's, from the characterisation of his attitudes and political involvement to the stories of his alleged whereabouts to the unbelievable story of the certificate issuing him his automatic rifle and ammunition, a certificate he first denied having any knowledge of, although it was presented to him by German authorities, then later attributed to a man in Prijedor. Then, when his brother attempted to cover for it, by claiming that he, Ljubo, had given it to the accused, the accused asserted that it was one of two documents that had been issued. Even in this, however, he and his brother were widely off as to the dates when his brother Ljubo supposedly provided this information to him. When you examine the alleged information provided by Mira and Ljubo Tadic, you must remember it is all a piece with the accused by family members determined to bolster each other's accounts. Are these insignificant details inconsistencies that can be attributed to the effect of the passage of time, to different ways of remembering, or are these deliberate lies told to protect this accused from criminal liabilities for his crimes during 1992? Your examination of the evidence and the reasonable inferences to be drawn from that evidence, we suggest, will show you that these were deliberate lies. When you evaluate all the evidence in this case, you will conclude that the credible evidence in the case proves the accused was an integral part of the crimes that were committed against non-Serbs in opstina Prijedor from May 1992 until December 1992. He was there in Kozarac at the beginning of the military attack on that town, helping to ensure that the shelling would hit designated targets. He was there when the town surrendered as part of the Serb forces rounding up the non-Serbs and forcibly expelling them from the town. He took part in calling out Muslim policemen and other Muslim men and killing them on 26th and 27th. He took part in separating out the men to be sent to various camps. He took part in the cleansing of villages around Kozarac, Sivci and the hamlet of Jaskici. He committed numerous offences in Keraterm and Omarska. He was frequently in these camps whose only purpose for existence was to beat, to torture, to kill, to terrorize non-Serbs. Most frequently, he was seen in the death camp at Omarska. His presence there is also proof of his continuing involvement in the ongoing persecution of non-Serbs. As he was there at the beginning of it all at the attack in Kozarac, so too was he there at the camp that was the end of it all for many non-Serbs. Trnopolje was the forced deportation centre for non-Serbs. His recurring presence there is further proof of his participation in, of his aiding and abetting of, of his encouragement and support of the persecution that occurred in opstina Prijedor in 1992. The Prosecution has met its burden in this case and in some instances, such as proof of widespread or systematic attack, has even gone beyond its burden in this case. Justice will be served in this case by finding the accused guilty as charged. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, Miss Hollis. Who will go forward with the Defence? I think you are pointing to whom, Mr. Wladimiroff? I think they are finished. I was trying to ask the interpreter whether they want a break, but I think they have told me to go forward. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, all members of the Defence will argue portions of our closing argument. As an introduction, I will submit to you some general observations about the case, and by doing so I hope to pave the road for the heart of the matter, the evidence in this case. It is Mr. Kay who will analyse the Prosecution evidence and Miss de Bertodano who will put forward the Defence case. Our arguments or evidence will be followed up by legal matters. Mr. Orie will discuss the character of the conflict with regard to the counts under Article 2 of the Statute. I will finally deal with the indictment, the scope of some crimes and the criminal responsibility and submit to you our overall conclusions. Now let me for my opening return in time to the first day of the trial. In their opening statements, your Honours, on May 7th, the Prosecution full of confidence stated that they had built up a very strong case against Dusko Tadic. Mr. Niemann, as Miss Hollis has done yesterday and today, gave a description of Tadic's conduct in 1992. It is a story of a man who, like a fanatic, is involved in all kinds of atrocities one after the other. What I noticed in May was the unrealistic picture that was given of Tadic, and that feeling did not change when Prosecution witnesses gave evidence. Miss Hollis confirmed this picture again yesterday and today. I wonder where that picture originated from. Is it the stereotypical bloodthirsty Serb as pictured so many times in war-crime stories by the other parties in the Bosnian conflict? I also wonder why this picture is so easily adopted by the Prosecution. We suggest, your Honours, that this picture has not been obtained from thorough and independent investigation on location. Apart from some sporadic visits to the locations where the camps used to be, the Prosecution did not carry out any investigation in the region itself. That was, apparently, not possible in 1994 and 1995. It was not until 1996 that the Prosecution was able to develop a number of general activities in the region. I still recall their complaints that in this respect they were in an even worse position than the Defence. So the Prosecution did not talk to any witness on the spot. They did not talk to people who were involved in the attack on Kozarac. They did not talk to people who were involved in the ethnic cleansing in the region. They did not speak with people who were involved in setting up and running the camps. In other words, the Prosecution did not hear any person who now lives in the region and who can tell what happened in 1992, not a single person. Who are the people then to whom the Prosecution talked, apart from the policy witnesses? What could be the force of the Prosecution's case against Dusko Tadic? The source has become very clear. It is exclusively the people who suffered as victims in the conflict between the ethnic groups in Bosnia. Exclusively? No, not quite, because apart from all Bosniacs, there was only one Serb who served as a source for the Prosecution's allegations. I will talk about this man separately at a later stage. So again, the Prosecution based their case against Dusko Tadic -- a member of one group involved in the Bosnian conflict -- on sources that originated more or less exclusively from the other party to the conflict. Listening to Mr. Niemann in May and to Miss Hollis yesterday and today, I do not get the impression that the Prosecution has given any thought to the consequences of this one-sided basis of their investigation and prosecution. For instance, I have not heard any indication that their own witnesses were tested with regard to their truthfulness. I have heard no indication whatsoever that the Prosecution carried out any investigation into the possibility that Dusko Tadic is not guilty of the charges in the indictment. On the contrary, the choice of witnesses that were eventually called to testify indicates that the Prosecution had only one thing in mind, that these witnesses alone were capable of telling the truth. But what about documentary evidence then? Nothing! Not a single investigation was carried out into written items of evidence that could shed some light on the accusations. The Prosecution only had at their disposal the documents that were seized in the Tadic's house in Munich. But these documents have no relevance to the question of guilt, which is the key issue in this procedure. So, there was not a full investigation to find out the most important matter in a criminal case, namely, the truth. Only the "other party" was heard and subsequently called. What is more, the Prosecution accepted that on this one-sided and shaky basis they could take a decision about the prosecution of Tadic. On this basis solely they have presented their case, and this is the basis of their assessment today that Dusko Tadic is guilty of all charges. One could, of course, argue that the Prosecution did not have the possibility to gather other probative material in addition to the evidence provided by witnesses, because again in 1994 and in 1995 they were unable to get into the region. In 1996, the local authorities were not cooperative, were they? We heard, indeed, today again about Simo Drljaca. That is correct, yes, but the conclusion does not alter: the Prosecution solely based its case on witnesses of the "other" party who were, indeed, available and they accepted this without sufficient backing up with documents as a sufficient basis for far-reaching conclusions about Tadic's guilt with respect to very serious crimes. Such a prosecution that is one-sided and incomplete is doomed to failure if this Court takes its task seriously, as we are confident it does. Because, let us be honest about it, matters like the one in issue are easy to solve. If you simply decide, as the Prosecution has, to believe the Prosecution witnesses, you can sentence Dusko Tadic for just about anything. The moment that one is mentally convinced that he did it and simply is looking for evidence that substantiates this, then it might technically not be difficult to convict Tadic, but we are confident you will not. Let us face it, did the testimony of witness L not sound very convincing? Did his statement not fit neatly into the Prosecution's picture? Was his statement not effectively corroborated by the Prosecution with all sorts of exhibits? Was this not the perfect final witness in the Prosecution's case? Did his evidence not paint a picture of the perfect stereotypical war criminal of whom we have all read? The Prosecution must have been firmly convinced by witness L with his stories of horrific, ethnically motivated crimes, otherwise they would not have called him to testify and would certainly not have saved him up to be the "final member of the show". That is the picture, your Honours. The Prosecution believed all its witnesses without query. That is what the Prosecution's case is: no clear investigation, but the gathering of accusations of members of the other ethnic group in the conflict. Does this mean that the Defence considers this other ethnic group -- in this case non-Serbs -- to be unworthy of belief or unreliable? No, that is certainly not the case. The fact that a witness comes from one or other ethnic group is as such no indication of their reliability. It is the specific circumstances of a group of people who have become victims of this terrible war which causes questions to be raised as the reliability as witnesses in a case where a member of the victorious group, their oppressors, is on trial. We have seen in the Demjanjuk case to what unjust and dramatic consequences this can lead. In my opening statement, I pointed out to you that there are witnesses who have adopted the accounts of their fellow prisoners or of friends or relatives. When inmates of the camps were released or moved to other locations, they talked to each other and their families and friends about their experiences. I also pointed out that we do not require the assistance of a psychologist to convince us of the importance and the power of suggestion. It is something you come across in everyday life. If several people witness the same event, they do not all recall every detail, but when they discuss events together afterwards, a composite story emerges. Rumour becomes truth. People convince themselves with ease that they have seen and heard things which they did not and could not have seen and heard. Having heard the evidence, we have good reason to believe that many people were told, either at the time or afterwards, that Tadic had been committing crimes in the camps. We have heard evidence about the impact of the Monika Gras film. People who have come across these rumours have fitted second-hand accounts into their own accounts to fill gaps or identify a person whom they did not, in fact, see at all. Meanwhile, we have heard the testimonies of the Prosecution witnesses and the fears I expressed in my opening statement have been realised. The witnesses you have heard giving evidence against Tadic have told stories, if not by hearsay, as a result either of an honest but distorted and false belief, or of prejudice against the Serb Dusko Tadic. In one case, the facts were proven to be even worse. witness L's false testimony was deliberately fabricated by the Bosnian authorities with no other objective than to secure the conviction of the Serb Dusko Tadic. When witness L finally confessed that he had lied, it became clear that information and video material exists which enables a non-witness to testify as though he had been there. His initial evidence was convincing to the extent that the Prosecution believed it without query. Witness L confessed that he had been set up by the Bosnian authorities after he was captured as a member of the Bosnian Serb Army. After being interviewed by the military and police officers about his own behaviour, he was transferred to (redacted). There at a security centre (that, as we now know turned out to be the building of the secret service of the Bosnian government) he was compelled to co-operate with the Bosnian authorities in testifying against Dusko Tadic. Witness L said that he was trained for a substantial length of time. They showed him all kinds of documents and maps, instructed him on the basis of the statements of others and showed him video tapes of Trnopolje camp and about Dusko Tadic. They instructed him to give statements while he was watching the video tapes. At the conclusion of the training, they gave him three prepared statements to sign. These statements were handed over to the Prosecution of the Tribunal. On the basis of this material, witness L gave evidence in Court, in closed session, as the anonymous Witness L. Further, it has become clear that the Prosecution did not in any way check whether witness L's statements were correct. This is in spite of the fact that for more than a year the man was at the Prosecution's disposal in the UN detention unit here in The Hague. It was not until we discovered, by coincidence, during our investigation on location information which indicated that witness L was not telling the truth, that the Prosecution reluctantly started to verify his statements. However, the Prosecution continued to the end to deny the results of the defence's investigation and to obstruct the Defence's attempts to expose witness L as a liar. Your Honours, experienced lawyers are always aware that the essential characteristic of the criminal procedure is that judges, prosecutors and defenders were not present at the indicted incidents and that, consequently, to answer the question as to whether a person is guilty they totally depend on the probative material presented. It is because of this that only the most reliable evidence is admissible to serve as a basis for justified decisions. So the issue in this case is the reliability of the probative material. It is your court that will have to decide whether or not probative material is reliable. There is no such thing as "partially reliable". The reliability of probative material is not a question of compromises. Probative material is reliable or not. For a proper International Criminal Tribunal, the issue is not how to satisfy the victims of violations of International Humanitarian Law, but to test whether the Prosecution has discharged itself of its burden of proof of the indictment. Miss Hollis, dealing with paragraph 9, stated that a reasonable inference could be made that the victim was alive at the time of alleged inhumane treatment, thereby reducing the standard of proof. We disagree. Beyond reasonable doubt requires more; it requires you to be sure, to be certain, that the evidence leaves no room for any doubt. A doubt raised not being speculative but reasonable makes the Court less than certain. It is this standard that is the standard to apply to the evidence adduced in support of the Defence alibi. We have nothing to prove. I submit to you that our evidence is not speculative but reasonable and sufficiently casts doubt upon a significant number of the Prosecution's allegations. Returning to the burden of proof of the Prosecution, I would like to address briefly the standard of sufficiency of proof. In the common law jurisdictions, uncorroborated evidence of a single witness may be sufficient to believe that a charge is proven beyond reasonable doubt. We have been discussing this standard in the context of the Defence motion on dismissal. You may remember that in civil law jurisdictions statutory provisions or case law take a different position. Some kind of independent causal corroboration is required there. These jurisdictions refer to this requirement with the so-called unis testis, nullius testis rule. The Tribunal works under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which rules are viewed to be a mixture of common law and civil law elements. That does not address this topic of the unis testis rule. The question therefore is ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if you would translate the Latin? You pronounce it in a continental fashion which is strange to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that, your Honour. It means one witness makes no proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As I said, the question now is raised whether the common law approach of uncorroborated evidence is a part of the international customary law. We submit that this is not the case. Under the circumstances of a trial with only witnesses that are personally involved as being parties to the conflict, it seems appropriate to the Defence not to accept the common law approach of non-corroboration, but instead to accept the civil law standard of sufficient corroboration. This argument has more weight since this trial is not a jury trial with a panel of 12 citizens, but a bench trial. The sufficiency of probative material is not a question of compromises. We submit that in a fair trial the standard of sufficiency of available material should not be manipulated to fit the need for a verdict. It is the duty of this criminal court to the international community to meet fair and settled standards of proof and not to develop ad hoc standards to enable it to convict. If the reliability of some probative material is affected by other information, that material must be disregarded. If there is any information that can affect the reliability of probative material, the Judges will have to convince themselves that it does not affect it, if they are to use that material as a basis for reaching a decision. If the Judges are unable to exclude the possibility that certain probative material is not reliable, they should dismiss that material from their minds. There must be no question of allowing unreliable material to prejudice the defendant in any way. So what is the information that affects the reliability of evidence? I already mentioned the most important factor in this case, the risk of prejudice of the Prosecution witnesses as members of the "other" ethnic group. This is the risk of hearing witnesses who were the victims of the conflict in Prijedor in which the Serbs were the aggressors and the victors; a conflict in which many or all of them lost family members, relatives and friends, as well as their homes and their livelihoods; and a conflict in which most of them were themselves imprisoned in camps. Can you exclude the possibility that the witnesses called by the Prosecution were prejudiced? I am afraid that you cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, if we are to consider that non-Serb witnesses, because of their ethnic background, are biased, then should we not also apply that standard to Serb witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will deal with that, your Honour. I am not saying that being a member of the "other" ethnic group as such is a sufficient criteria. It is the matter of being imprisoned and attached by the conflict, having lost family members or having lost your homes or having been driven out of the area. That makes them a risk. As I said, can you exclude, your Honours, the possibility that the witnesses called by the Prosecution were prejudiced? I am afraid you cannot. Moreover, it is important to realise that many of the them talked to each other about the traumas of 1992, not only in the camps themselves, but also thereafter. What also played a role is that many of them subsequently lived in the same region after they had left former Yugoslavia. This was exacerbated by the fact that soon after 1992 the media began to play its role in relaying stories about what had happened in opstina Prijedor all over the globe. It is an established fact that the events of 1992 and, in particular, the alleged activities of Dusko Tadic were discussed both publicly and among the witnesses who have come to give evidence at his trial. Against the background of the evidence given by Mr. Reid showing that most -- it is about 45 per cent, if I remember well -- of the Prosecution witnesses live in Germany, Mr. Deichmann's testimony has made clear to what extent this case was publicised in Germany since 1992. It is hard to resist the conclusion that the extensive media coverage was simply unavoidable for those witnesses at least. I return to the basic principle concerning reliability of evidence which I stated a few moments ago. Can one exclude the possibility that these witnesses were affected by all the publicity and by all those stories within their own circles? I draw the Court's attention to, for example, the pictures as shown by Mr. Deichmann during his evidence, Exhibit D102B. I am afraid that no one can exclude this, and this leads to serious questions as to whether the evidence of these witnesses can be reliable. It is our submission that it cannot be, and is not. Does this mean that the Defence contends that all the Prosecution witnesses are lying? In witness L's case, this was proved to be so certainly. In many other cases, we have good reason to believe that witnesses were not telling the truth, and that they adjusted their accounts of their experiences to fit the Prosecution's case. Time after time we have shown that witnesses had given previous statements which were totally at variance with the accounts they gave in Court. It may be that there were also witnesses who were honest but mistaken and that their honest mistakes led to the fabrication of others. The motivation to call someone to account for the loss of a friend or members of a family is great.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, will you tell us which witnesses you consider have given testimony at variance or will Mr. Kay do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kay will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He will be handling the Prosecution case, OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution, your Honours, has suggested that inconsistencies of the witnesses might be caused by interpretation problems. We do not believe so. The professional interpreters have shown to be very capable. The difficulties we have witnessed were of a very minor character and did not affect the substance of the testimony. We have not witnessed any relevant misinterpretation. Interpreters may misinterpret a word, but it is highly unlikely that they would insert a passage in a statement which bears no relation to anything a witness said, as Elvir Grozdanic, for example, alleges. Another example is the Prosecution alleging that in incidents such as the chicken kiosk incident where Sulejman Besic gave a statement which did not mention the accused, there also is an interpretation problem. It certainly is an interpretation problem; the interpretation being where the witness is telling the truth or not. Anyhow, we submit to the Court that there is not a proper showing of relevant misinterpretations as alleged by the Prosecution. As I already said, your Honours, all these details will be discussed at length by Mr. Kay when he is dealing with the evidence in detail. We will submit that these indications, together with the probable contamination of the testimony, will lead you to the conclusion that the evidence of the Prosecution witnesses is insufficiently reliable to provide the basis for a conviction. More generally, I have already pointed out that, against the background of Mr. Deichmann's testimony, it is highly improbable that almost none of the Prosecution witnesses watched television or saw newspapers during the past years. The fact that the huge majority of them denied in evidence that they had received any information from the media is an indication that the witnesses feel that they need to boost their own credibility. With respect to the Defence witnesses, this was not the case. Almost all Defence witnesses stated honestly that they had seen reports about this case in the newspapers and on television. The impact of these unreliable statements of the Prosecution witnesses about their knowledge of the media coverage is even more significant where it concerns the four witnesses who identified Tadic on the basis of the photospread. For the differences between relevant identification and the meaningless recognition, I refer to the testimony of Professor Wagenaar. The identification witnesses are Senad Muslimovic, Zemka Sabhaz, Kasim Mesic and Sead Halvadzic and not, as Miss Hollis submitted yesterday, Witness S -- Witness R. Witness R admitted that he knew Dusko Tadic. Then we also have Draguna Jaskic. What do we make out of that? What do we make from her statement regarding this witness and what do we make with her reactions to the photospread or, should I say, her alleged reactions to the photospread, because the only information we have about that is her own statement about how she reacted, and we have additional information about that from a witness who was an inexperienced law enforcement officer. I say inexperienced because he had never performed a photo test before. We submit that the position of the Prosecution regarding this witness is speculative when they say that her reaction may be understood as a positive identification. Professor Wagenaar made it clear that her reactions were insufficient to accept this witness as a positive identification witness. With regard to the four others, the evidence given by them as to their lack of knowledge of the image of Tadic was not an impressive indicator of their reliability, not only because, as was shown by the evidence given by Mr. Reid, the four tests were made after the highly publicized start of the trial, just before the person in question was about to testify before the Court, but also because no strict, flowed procedures were used; procedures that fundamentally breached the basic rules that ought to apply to a photo identification if it is to be regarded as reliable. The Prosecution contends that the photo array was approved by Professor Wagenaar. That is not exactly what Professor Wagenaar wrote in his letter and what he told us in evidence. I refer to Exhibit D90. Hence, that he made a reservation as to the ethnic background of the foils. Mr. Reid told us that nine out of 13 were from the former Yugoslavia, but he did not tell us where from the former Yugoslavia. Were they from Macedonia, from Slovenia, from Croatia, from Bosnia, from Serbia, from Montenegro? We simply do not know. The testimony of Professor Wagenaar shows that people might think that ethnic differences are not relevant, but they might be wrong about this simply because, so witness Professor Wagenaar, they are not aware of their ability to recognise the ethnic differences of foils of a photospread. The Prosecution also contends that no gross deficiencies have occurred. We disagree. Let us focus then on these persons who say they identified Dusko Tadic: Senad Muslimovic claims that he saw Tadic in the context of paragraph 6 in the hangar of Omarska camp. This witness left the area ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I just interrupt you? Are you moving now away from the four who looked at the photospread or are you continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am talking about the four.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Senad Muslimovic is one of them, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Go ahead. Do not let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The witness left the area after the conflict and lived in Slovenia, in Austria and elsewhere in Europe before he emigrated to [redacted]. Where he now lives you will find in evidence on page 6431 up to 6432. He claims that he did not know Dusko Tadic before the war. Despite all the publicity in the countries where he lived, he denies having read about Tadic in newspapers or having seen his picture on television. However, we know that he was fully aware of the trial when he was shown the photospread. We have that in evidence by the statement of Mr. Reid. This witness was interviewed by Mr. Ackheim of the Office of the Prosecutor on 26th March of this year. On 9th May of this year, two days after the actual trial started with full publicity around the world (and in this context, seeing the place where the man lives, I specifically mention the daily coverage by [redacted] Mr. Safer showed him the book of photographs. Mr. Safer may have had written instructions, that may follow from the evidence of Mr. Reid, but these instructions were not produced so we know nothing about it. A brief description of these instructions is in evidence. I will come back to that. As the witness was aware of the trial, Mr. Safer varied the instructions. That is in evidence too. We do not know how. Mr. Reid could not tell us. The notes, if any, of Mr. Safer were not produced and no recording of times was made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, before you go on, Mr. Wladimiroff, Mr. Muslimovic, is that the gentleman who was from [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: [redacted], your Honour, now you mention it -- I tried to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. The reason I was asking was that I wanted to know about [redacted]. We have our 30 minutes that we can work on. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The next one, your Honour, is Zemka Sahbaz. She claims that she saw Dusko Tadic in the context of paragraph 12 in Jaskici. This witness also left the area after the conflict and lives now in a (redacted) country, which country you will find on page 3018. The witness claims not to have known Tadic before the war, and she totally denies reading newspapers at all or watching television at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you now? She comes from one of the two villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It is your pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, my pronunciation is always a problem, your Honour. Sometimes I even do not understand myself! But, nevertheless, I hope you were able to follow my argument. This witness, your Honours, was interviewed by Mr. Ackheim of the Office of the Prosecutor on 31st May of this year.
