The book of photographs was shown to her by Mr. Ackheim on the same day, after the trial had been broadcast worldwide on a daily basis for about three weeks. Also, in this case we only have a global description from Mr. Reid of the way the photo test was generally applied. We do not know how it was applied to this witness. The test was not applied according to a protocol. No notes were made and there was no recording of times. The next witness here is Kasim Mesic. This witness claims that he saw Dusko Tadic in the context of paragraph 4 in Omarska. This witness left the area and his present residence is kept secret from the Court and the Defence. The Prosecution refused to release to the Defence in confidence the town and country in which the witness lives. According to the evidence of Mr. Reid, though, this witness may live in [redacted]. Page 6411. The witness claims that he did not know Tadic and he also denies having read about Tadic in newspapers or having seen his picture on television. After his interview by the Office of the Prosecutor in January of this year, he was shown the book of photographs by Mr. Ackheim during the trial on 12th June of this year. Here too we only have a global description from Mr. Reid of the way the photo test was generally applied. We do know, however, some details of how it was applied to this witness. I quote from the transcript, pages 6408 to 6409. Question: "When he first handed you the book, what did he tell you to do when he first handed you the book?" Answer: "Well, whether I recognised here in the book who was that Tadic whom I recognised". Question: "When he handed you the book, did he tell you to look for the man Tadic? Is that what he told you to do? Did he use that name?" Answer: "No. No. No, only 'Do you recognise that picture and which you thought was Tadic?' I do not remember exactly. No, he asked me to recognise among, to try to identify him among all those men who was the man". May I emphasise, your Honours, "which you thought was Tadic". We further know from the hearsay evidence or second-hand information given by Mr. Reid, because he was not present during the test, that the test was not applied according to a protocol, no notes were made and there was not a recording of times. The last witness of these four is Sejad Halvadzic. This witness claims that he has seen Dusko Tadic in the context of paragraph 4 in the military barracks of Prijedor. Also this witness left the area and his present residence is also kept secret from the Court and the Defence, as I outlined earlier. According to the statement of Mr. Reid, the witness may live in [redacted]. Page 6411. The witness claims that he did not know Tadic before the war and again we heard the familiar story. He did not read newspaper reports about Tadic. He did not see his picture on television. After interview by the OTP on 4th May last year, the book of photographs was shown to the witness by Mr. Ackheim during the trial on 14th June this year. Once again, we only have a global description from Mr. Reid on the way the photo test was generally applied. We do not know how it was applied to this witness. However, we know, as in the previous cases, the test was not applied according to a protocol. No notes were made and no recording of times. From what we know about the photo test, we submit that you must find that the procedure was not carried out in accordance with the basic rules that ought to be applied to a reliable photo identification. It has become abundantly clear that the procedures used were fatally flawed and we further submit that you cannot be certain, indeed, that it is highly unlikely, that at the time of these tests the witnesses had not been exposed, consciously or unconsciously, to the image of Dusko Tadic. After Professor Wagenaar's extensive comments, it is also unnecessary to stress that the so-called dock IDs have no significant evidentiary meaning. Those who knew Tadic have indicated that they still know him. It does not say anything about the correctness of their other statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, with respect to the four, are you finished with the four now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I recall Dr. Wagenaar's testimony (and I do not have a transcript cite with me), he testified that even if the 50 rules that he talked about, if the rules had been violated, that would not invalidate the test but would only make it of less value. That is how I recall his testimony. Can you help me in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a general statement, that is a fair representation of what he told us. But I may also draw your attention to those portions of the evidence where he explained that flawed procedures may lead to unreliable evidence in this matter. Because if, for example, the photos were shown by someone who is aware who is the accused, the evidence shows that the one who is showing, the officer who is administering the photo test, might indicate, therefore, to the witness to whom the test is applied who might be in the photospread as a relevant person. So he gave more examples where the procedure, if not correctly administered, might result in unreliable evidence. So here the issue is, again as what I have said before, is evidence reliable or are there reasons to believe that you cannot exclude that the evidence was obtained in a way that makes it unreliable? I am arguing here that you cannot exclude that, because we have no firm evidence provided by the Prosecution that these procedures were correct and no faults, no mistakes, were made. On the other hand, we have suggested to you, not speculative but to a reasonable standard, that we have good reason to believe that they were not correctly administered. Therefore, there is room for doubt whether these pieces of evidence are reliable. We believe they are not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I just thought that he was here to testify with respect to the validity of the test, and that that was his expertise. I was really trying to recall what his conclusion was. At first, his conclusion was that he could not say that the procedures used by the Prosecutor were not valid because he did not know the procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He could not tell whether it was valid or invalid.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that, because he did not know. Then he gave us 50 rules that we went through very carefully. Though after we went through them, I thought it was his conclusion that, even if they had been violated as to these four, it would not invalidate the test but would just make it of "less value", as I recall the exact words. Those were for the four. Then for the others, he had no challenge to the ID, the other dock identifications. Is that how you recall it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As to the four, what I recall, he did not make an assessment of the four, whether specific mistakes would lead to the reliability or unreliability of the evidence. He was simply not in a position to make an assessment on that matter. What we do here is give our assessment which fits in his evidence where he told us that if certain mistakes are made, then it will affect the reliability of the evidence. We suggest to you that these mistakes may have been made or we have good reason to believe that they have been made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand. OK. Yes, Miss Hollis, are you standing not to interrupt Mr. Wladimiroff but for a redaction?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think we have accomplished that redaction.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I have several, if I could perhaps tell you which ones I have? It is page 6695 line 7; 6696 lines 1, 2 and 3; 6697 line 10; 6698 line 12. These are all locations, your Honour. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. To summarise it, it is our position that the Prosecution failed to show that the procedures in these four cases were without any mistake. On the contrary, we have argued that there are good reasons to believe that mistakes were made. From the evidence of Mr. Reid, your Honours, we know that out of nine persons eight persons made a positive identification and one did not. The Prosecution prefers, however, to produce only four of the witnesses. Therefore, we do not know anything about the quality of identification of the four others. We were not able to cross-examine them. Apparently, they were not very convincing otherwise the Prosecution would certainly have called them to testify. We submit, therefore, that these witnesses invalidly identified a person who the Prosecution claim to be Dusko Tadic. Alternatively, the procedure of the photo test was so poor that the Prosecution preferred not to produce that kind of flawed evidence. From the second-hand information of Mr. Reid, we may assume that the witnesses have been shown the photospread during an average time of three minutes. Actually we do not know how much time in reality the four presented witnesses saw the photo array. Professor Wagenaar explained that the time of showing is relevant for the reliability of the test. I may add to this that the assumption of the Prosecution that prior exposure of Tadic will not harm the identification is totally speculative and certainly contrary to the evidence of Professor Wagenaar. It is not a matter of choice to be made by the witness or the Prosecution to proclaim that seeing Mr. Tadic's image on television or in the media does not invalidate a claim of seeing him before at the scene of the crime. The truth is that we simply do not know, and that prior exposure raises substantial or at least reasonable doubt about the reliability of the identification on the basis of the photospread. We simply do not know ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, can you tell me, why do you assume that the Prosecution proceeds on that basis, that prior exposure will not have a deleterious effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I heard Miss Hollis arguing that even if Dusko Tadic had seen -- I mean, the four witnesses may have seen the image of Dusko Tadic before, that such a circumstance will not affect their identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see. I had not picked that up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As I said, the truth is that we simply do not know how long each of the photospreads were shown to the witness, and we do not know whether they have seen him before, though we have good reasons to believe that they have seen Dusko Tadic before. I explained to you that such a circumstance casts doubt, at least reasonable doubt, about reliability of the identification on the basis of the photospread. We simply do not know whether ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, but can we just discuss that for a moment? Are you saying that previous exposure converts what would be an identification into a recognition?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Or does it merely make it a poor quality identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We need more to make that .....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You need to know the extent of exposure, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, so from the simple, the mere circumstance that he might have seen or has seen him does not enable us to make assessment whether he is a recognition witness or a kind of crippled identification witness. We simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But the main message here, the important message, is, though, that you cannot rely on this evidence to place the accused on the scene of the crime. I was going to say that we simply do not know whether the witness identifies an image he has seen before from the newspapers or television or, as he claims, from the scene of the crime. The truth is that he simply does not know or that he is not aware from where he knows the image. Therefore, we need more information to make an assessment and we cannot. Another issue raised by the Prosecution is the reasoning of the Prosecution witnesses who claim not to have watched television or to have read newspapers or magazines. The Defence is not convinced by the argument that these witnesses simply explained this by saying they were "not interested by what happened in the former Yugoslavia". We suggest that all Prosecution witnesses were quite willing to testify because they were very motivated to talk and that, therefore, they were fully aware of what happened in the former Yugoslavia. They were certainly not naive persons with no idea of the present reality. They were very well informed witnesses who, in almost all cases, were personally involved and well motivated to testify. In addition to comments on the one-sidedness and other shortcomings in the Prosecution's case, I should like to make a general observation about the questions raised with regard to the reliability of the Prosecution witnesses during cross-examination. Witness by witness you have been able to form an idea about the aspects that could affect the reliability. That applies also, of course, to the cross-examination of the Defence witnesses. However, there is a significant difference. As regards the Prosecution witnesses, the Defence during cross-examination mainly focused on the description of the incident about which the evidence was given. This cross-examination showed that there are many contradictions or discrepancies. We will address this subject in detail when we discuss the evidence. On the other hand, the Prosecution's cross-examination was mainly directed at the unrelated activities of the Defence witness himself, or his family and personal circumstances. The substance of what the witness said in support of the alibi was not, on the whole, undermined by cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, do you think perhaps that might be explained by the fact that the Trial Chamber denied the Prosecution access to Defence witness statements? Of course, you had the witness statements which Mr. Kay used very effectively throughout. When I say "effectively", continuously throughout the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not discussing here the whys of things in this context ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I know you are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- your Honour, and may I point out again that we had access to the German file and that enabled us to use prior statements. That was a different position to a disclosure obligation of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are correct. You have not said why. I am suggesting why, and asking you whether there was any other attack that was made by the Defence on the substance of the Prosecution testimony other than statements. As I recall it, it was repeated use of statements. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I am arguing here is what I argued at the very beginning, whatever the reasons might be for not being able to conduct a full, thorough and independent investigation in this matter, the fact is that the Prosecution did not. As I indicated at the very beginning of my closing argument, they were not able to go into the area. They did not speak to people. That is the reality. Whatever the reasons might have been, it is the reality that they did not. Here too it is reality.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is true, but they did attempt to talk to your witnesses before. We made every effort to encourage the two of you to get together, of course. Your witnesses, as they have the right to, chose not to talk with the Prosecutor. So, in terms of the substance of what the Defence witnesses would testify to, that is something that they did not have access to by way of statement or in terms of just talking with the witnesses before. But I think you are correct. Why is not important. It is a fact, but I think it is just a fairer presentation of it, if that is made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If we are going to discuss that again, your Honour, I may recall that we, or at least Mr. Kay and Miss de Bertodano, were always on their feet even in cases where we only had a two or three line proverb. We always examined on the issue, on the incident, not on the person.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, however you lawyers wish to handle it, there are books written on cross-examination; sometimes you use a prior statement, sometimes you use motive, you use whatever. Mr. Kay probably knows because he is the expert in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But, in any case, we will hear from him about the inconsistencies and I will ask him what is the basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. As I was dealing with the substance of what the Defence witnesses were saying in support of the alibi and that, as a whole, the substance of that evidence was not undermined by cross-examination of the Prosecution. I have mentioned the word or the term "alibi". Since I have mentioned that, I should point out that the Defence, indeed, succeeded in gathering objective documentary evidence, the duty rosters. It is significant that neither in cross-examination nor in rebuttal the reliability of these documents was seriously doubted. I emphasise, for example, that the rebuttal witness, Fikret Kadiric, was not even asked about Exhibit D66, in spite of the fact that he himself co-operated in preparing of the book and his name was signed at the bottom of one of the pages. In my opening statement I said that the Prosecution of Dusko Tadic started under unfavourable circumstances. The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was still going on at that time. It was not until this year that the Defence was able to conduct an investigation into the extremely scanty and unreliable documentary information that had become available in the beginning of 1995. It was not until this year that we got access to the actual duty rosters administration and that we could receive "redacted" copies. It was not until October, during the video link, that we could obtain the complete copies. We produced all that material. It was not until this year that we were able to actually carry out an effective investigation. However, a large number of constraints still remained. For instance, due to lack of co-operation on the part of authorities, it remained a problem to trace witnesses. It was difficult to find people willing to disclose information to the Defence. It was even more difficult to persuade people to actually testify as witness before the Tribunal. There were too many cases in which the authorities forbade witnesses to speak with us or forbade witnesses to testify. I may remind you of the ban issued by Simo Drljaca and sustained by the Minister of Home Affairs. Taking into account the attitude of the Prijedor authorities and, more generally, the way in which the Tribunal is regarded in Republic Srpska, we admire the people who showed the courage to come to The Hague and to testify or to come on the video link and to testify. Without them, a fair trial would not have been possible. But, the Court must bear in mind at all times that we were only able to hear a limited number of witnesses. We were unable to persuade many witnesses whom we considered crucial for the Defence case to testify. For instance, it appeared to be impossible to hear within the framework of the Tribunal vital evidence from the people who actually worked in Omarska and Keraterm. There were still many other parts of the indictment that required further investigation, but in respect of which it appeared impossible without the necessary legal tools to talk to the persons concerned or to persuade them to testify. We have come to realise that important information has been withheld from your Court. It must be said that this is inherent to the legal foundation for this Tribunal. You, Judges, cannot do anything upon your own powers, the Defence even less. In this respect, everybody depends entirely on the co-operation of states. I still remember the discussion within the framework of the jurisdiction concerning the question as to whether Republika Srpska is, indeed, a state. Here we are confronted with the fact that a non-existing state cannot be expected to give its co-operation. The negation of Republika Srpska had a very negative effect on the Tadic case, both for the Defence and for the Prosecution. This brings us back to square one and to the reason of the one-sidedness of the evidentiary material of the Prosecution case. Let me, therefore, conclude my introduction with the statement that this trial took place under unfavourable circumstances. There were insufficient possibilities to fundamentally investigate the truth, neither by the Prosecution, nor by the Defence. You will have to make do with the witnesses who press charges on account of their personal involvement, whilst the Defence is limited as regards the possibilities to provide counter evidence. But I stress from the outset that any inadequacies must not be used to the prejudice of the defendant. It must always be at the forefront of your minds that it is for the Prosecution to discharge itself of the burden of proving that the defendant committed the crimes alleged. It cannot be held against Dusko Tadic that evidence crucial for his defence was, through no fault of his own, unavailable to this Court. Your Honour, it seems to be an appropriate moment because I will now beg you to allow Mr. Kay and Miss de Bertodano to analyse the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one question -- I will ask you this before the recess -- you indicated that you would speak to criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We had asked counsel to address in their submissions Article 7.1 and we have not received anything from the Defence. Are you going to speak orally to criminal responsibility under 7.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will deal with that matter orally.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that after Mr. Kay speaks, because I understand you have finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After Mr. Kay's analysis of the Prosecution case, Miss de Bertodano will deal with the Defence case, as I said, and Mr. Orie will discuss the character of the conflict. Then I will finally deal with the indictment, criminal responsibility, and all that kind of legal matters.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, I will wait until then and expect that you will address Article 7.1. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you like to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Let us start, first of all, with some background allegations that have been made concerning the character of Dusko Tadic before the conflict in Kozarac. In many respects, the Prosecution have presented certain incidents that happened in the period from 1989 to 1992 as revealing the character of a man who was, putting it bluntly, anti-Muslim or ill-disposed to those Muslim residents within Kozarac and with whom he had lived, apparently contentedly, for many years. The first feature of this evidence is the so-called threatening letter. Curiously, this was a document that I do not think was produced during the trial. It seems to have been received by Mr. Tadic at a time when there was, perhaps, rising ethnic consciousness in the region and in the former Yugoslavia, and at a time when for the first time people were identifying themselves with political parties which, ironically, all appear to have split under ethnic lines, SDS being mainly representative of the Serb people, SDA being mainly representative of the Muslim people, and following and supporting their aspirations. One wonders at this time in 1989 what possible reason that Dusko Tadic would have had in writing this letter himself and sending it to a newspaper in Belgrade. At this time there is no evidence that he was a member of the SDS. There is no evidence that he had become involved in politics, and to try to inspire in some way antipathy to himself as a Serb living in Kozarac, we suggest has no possible foundation and no reasonable support as an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I notice you say "and sending it to Belgrade". I know the suggestion that he wrote it himself, but I had thought that the leaking of the letter was not attributed by anyone to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was said in evidence at one stage, and I hope the Court forgives me for not remembering the passage exactly, that it was printed in a newspaper ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- in Belgrade and ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But it was not suggested ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- in that way achieved prominence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- that he had a hand in that, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it was in one passage of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought that the suggestion was that Mrs. Tadic had written it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have had both suggestions, that Mrs. Tadic wrote it, Mr. Tadic wrote it and, in those circumstances, it seems almost as though those who did not like him or felt that there was an explanation that was required to be given were reversing the situation to the recipient of the letter: "Oh, that is nothing to do with us, our people did not write that letter. He probably wrote it himself". That is a curious way of approaching such a problem, in this curious way that this letter was supposedly something that he was to have produced. But there we have it. It seems to have been something that was a feature within Kozarac life and Kozarac society. Everyone knew about it. We believe that the presentation of this particular evidence in this form as being a way of presenting Dusko Tadic in a bad light is unfair and has no logical support, because one then considers the other aspect of his standing in the local community which was his cafe that he opened and built. One wonders why someone opening a business in the middle of Kozarac, which was a 95 per cent Muslim dominated area, and the evidence has it that the centre was particularly dominated by the Muslim community, would seek to potentially upset and turn away all his potential customers. Again, there is no logic in that. These assertions that he ran a cafe that made certain people within the community unwelcome, in our submission, is wrong. There was a suggestion somewhere in the evidence that, in fact, perhaps local Muslims boycotted it. Again this is an example of a turning around of something that was happening within Kozarac, and an unfair interpretation being put on people's own behaviour against this man that has been stressed within the evidence that does not do him justice? There was no doubt that at the time of the beginning of 1992 people were passing through Kozarac as the troops were being drawn from the Croatian front, and military personnel were obviously in the area in far greater numbers than they had been before. But one wonders why, if this was a cafe that excluded so many people or made them unwelcome, so many of the Prosecution witnesses seem to have frequented it, and so many seem to have been the only Muslim who would go into the cafe. Clearly, in our submission, there is an attempt here to paint the picture of a man who was in conflict with those people who were Muslims in his local community that does him less than justice. We now turn to politics and his membership of the SDS which the Prosecution have presented as a key feature of his standing in terms of the ethnic cleansing of the Kozarac area, and his able to take up positions of power later on in the year. It is quite clear from the evidence that the SDS had no party base or effective power base within Kozarac until much later, in August and September 1992 does a local party start to become organised. It is quite clear that the referendum that was established in November 1991 was not a well-run, efficiently organised affair. There were just over 100 voters who voted in it on the polling day. It is quite clear that there is no access here by Dusko Tadic at a very local level to the organisation that one might expect that the main party in Prijedor could have given him. The fact that he is chosen to be the returning officer or supervise the referendum on that day, in our submission, does not provide a full enough picture of the political fanatic that the Prosecution have attempted to explain him as being when one considers the bare facts. We listened to much evidence concerning the political philosophy of the SDS and publications by various of their advisers or gurus, if I can call them that, but none of that in any way has been connected to Dusko Tadic. There is no indication that he was either learned or active in the SDS beyond a very local level, and at a level that is contrary to how the Prosecution are presenting his image as someone who would be prepared fanatically to pursue and implement their policy of the ethnic cleansing of the area. In absolute contrary distinction of this, we have his role in the so-called League of Peace in May 1992 when various citizens, not connected with political parties, deliberately banded themselves together to go to Prijedor to negotiate on behalf of the people within Kozarac to try to get a peaceful solution to the problems that were manifesting themselves as between Prijedor and Kozarac after the Serb takeover of power on April 29th. It is interesting that the local citizens chose Dusko Tadic, one would have thought not because he was going to be a destructive influence, but that Kemal Susic who knew him well thought that it would be a positive role that he could play. One of the other members of that group chose, perhaps, to criticise his role later, and say that he did not provide the local priest and get him back into Kozarac. But again is this an example of blame being put on this man for something that he was not in a position to achieve? The simple fact of the matter remains that that group of citizens chose to use him and he went along with their attempt at reconciliation to a degree that shows, in our submission, that this was not a man embarking on a conflict against those people he had lived with for so many years, but a man trying to achieve the best solution to Kozarac that was the place that he had grown up in, that he loved greatly and where his business was. That is, in many respects, a significant point for the Defence, that he was to a degree popular within Kozarac. He did have himself a great commitment to the life of the town. If he was aware of what was going to happen to Kozarac, one wonders why he permits his brother to open up a business at the beginning of May and have a delivery of alcohol only two or three days before the conflict started and, in those circumstances, put finances, goods, at risk. It just does not fit the picture. To say he was going to be aware of the conflict on May 24th is, in fact, not looking at this evidence closely enough to see what he had at stake within the town and to see what his own conduct and behaviour was like. It was tried to be said against him that he was aware that something was going to happen. Many of those Muslim residents and citizens of Kozarac were aware that something was going to happen. Kemal Susic said that himself in his evidence. Everyone had a feeling that something was going to happen. Hence, Muslims as well as Serb families were seeking to leave the region to avoid what was going to eventually occur. I dare say no one expected things to turn out quite as they did, but there was this great feeling that something was going to happen. Citing disputes in cafes between two men, complaints about young men being involved in sexual relations with the niece as being examples of extreme behaviour, provocative behaviour, against Muslim residents, or having a dispute over some parking ticket as a reason for embarking upon most extreme behaviour possible in relation to that community, in our submission, shows rather the bottom of the barrel being scraped rather than hard and substantial evidence being put before this court of behaviour that one would expect would fit the profile that the Prosecution have attempted to build. Again, when one looks at his later behaviour in the year of being involved with the Red Cross, of work within Kozarac and the Local Commune, that implies a man helping his town and behaviour that is consistent with the way he had led his life for so many years. The church incident that was supposed to have happened at some stage round about March, maybe April 1992, derives from the evidence of Witness Q, and about him I will tell the Court more later. We have a problem here as to the reliability of this evidence. Young children who had been standing guard duty near the Serb Orthodox church coming to complain to Witness Q and fellow people on checkpoint duty near the hospital at a time when it was almost midnight, and the adult who had been down there near the church on guard duty himself not coming to inform Witness Q over what happened, one wonders why, if this was right, and not excited imaginations running riot, young people out too late doing something that, perhaps, they were not suited to do in an area where there is a lot of anxiety and there are tensions and their imaginations get the better of them, one wonders why they did not go down to the police station, why they happened to go to see Witness Q. About this incident, one wonders how on earth they were able to see a man coming to the back of the church with a canister of petrol. The Court has heard evidence about the lighting at the front of the church. The witness himself had to concede that there were no lights at the back of the church. We have also heard evidence about the state of the lighting, what it was like. In many respects, this incident, as described by Witness Q, was rather making Dusko Tadic into the bogey man of Kozarac that these young people were, perhaps, imagining and giving such a report if, indeed, it was true or accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Kay, I recall that testimony because I remember that that was our first discussion back and forth about hearsay -- if it was not the first, it certainly was a long discussion -- but I also seem to recall that there was an adult who confirmed that incident other than Q. Am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was a man called Besic and he was on duty at the time, but Q confirmed to me he did not actually speak to Besic. He spoke to another adult who, I think, was the parent or father of one of the children. That is as far as the evidence got. The sighting was by the children who were on this guard duty. I am much obliged, your Honour. If we turn now to the indictment, Witness Q, who has been spoken of by me in relation to the background, is really the Prosecution witness who kicks off these allegations within the indictment because of the lighting of the flares on 24th May between 8.00 to 9 o'clock in the evening during the attack on Kozarac. Paragraph 4.1 of the indictment largely reflects many of the allegations made by this particular witness. It is curious for this reason: how did Dusko Tadic get into Kozarac during the shelling of the town? What on earth would he be doing lighting flares in an area between the hospital and his own house which would have every chance of getting his own house bombed as much as the shelling of the hospital? It is very odd that during the shelling of Kozarac when there are no other reports of any form of insurgency by the military who are conducting this operation that for some reason he with one other, named as Bosko Dragicevic, would enter the town and do something such as this. It is also ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, you say "no other reports of insurgency"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Going into the town and taking part in the conflict during this period. Our first report of troops appear to be 26th May, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did not Mr. Tadic testify he saw a tank earlier and went with the priest to see about it? That was before they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that is before the attack on Kozarac. This is a planned military operation. There is no doubt about it. The shelling happens at 2 o'clock in the afternoon and then the troops go in later, which is a classical movement, but there is no evidence of any other form of insurgency during this period. One wonders why you would be sending people in in this way and putting themselves at risk of being hit by shells. You also wonder why on earth the artillery would not have had the correct sighting from where they were firing these shells if they wanted to bomb the hospital or bomb any other building within Kozarac. Perhaps the lack of sophistication in this passage of Witness Q's testimony rather exposes it for what it is. We suggest to the Court that it was a made-up story. There is every indication of it being made up because of the contradiction of his evidence in this Court with what he had said previously in a statement. I will remind the Court of what he said in his previous statement, that the shelling started after he had had his lunch, that he took cover and in the evening went up to the hospital and saw the incident relating to the flares. No electricity, of course, in Kozarac at this time. It must have been a very dark place, but still he claims to have seen this. His evidence before the Court was that he went up to the hospital after he had had his lunch. He was on duty at the hospital from that period until that time between 8.00 to 9 o'clock in the evening, and then walked down from the hospital to return to his home to see what was happening within Kozarac town. We have heard a lot of talk about the value of inconsistent statements, the problems with interpretation, but this is a completely different picture, completely different periods and passages of time. One account has him leaving home at night and seeing it; the other has him leaving the hospital and coming back to the home and seeing it. There are a number of other unanswered questions about this testimony, because the next identification of Dusko Tadic in the region, coincidentally also by Witness Q, is the morning of 26th May. So one wonders what he was doing during this period of time from 24th May, having allegedly lit a flare so that the hospital could be bombed, until that period of 26th May, some 36 plus hours. Where was he? What was he doing? Why would he be there? Or has this statement, which we suggest is fabricated, been put before this Court for emotive reasons, and the fact that Dusko Tadic's house is quite near the hospital is, perhaps, an inconvenience for this particular witness, but the hospital has such emotive connotations it is guaranteed to bring horror to those listening to evidence, to those listening to his account, that it can instinctively invoke prejudice. There are other examples of this within this witness's testimony. A man stabbed so that he was stuck against the door of a house, a child killed by a pitchfork, another gruesome killing in some particular way of which I will just remind myself now -- a head on a bayonet. If one looks at the context of this witness's evidence with these extreme allegations, regretfully, we submit to this Court, that this is not a witness helping this Court with the truth and the facts. This is a witness who is trying to prejudice the Court, to prejudice the Court and anyone else who will listen, against the Serbs and against Dusko Tadic who was a Serb. That statement of his about 24th May and the firing of the flares just does not make sense. The flaws that I have put before the Court concerning the fact that the artillery you would have thought would have been able to hit the hospital if they had wanted to, the fact that he has given inconsistent statements and the fact that this witness claims to have seen all this in a state of darkness, and when there is a great gap in time, we suggest, puts his evidence into that category that the Court should reject. As I said, the next sighting is, indeed, by Witness

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this matter, there is a further example that he is prepared to make up stories within his testimony if it suits his purposes to try to bolster his credibility. This concerns the morning of 26th May down at the triangle at the bottom of Marsala Tita Street, and the allegation which is set out in the indictment here of the beating of two policemen. In fact, in his evidence he only gave evidence of one beating of one policeman and, in our observations on the indictment, we made this point to the Court for them to note in relation to any findings that there may be. He is down in the centre of Kozarac in that morning of 26th May with a kalashnikov rifle dressed in a military uniform as the convoy of people had come down Marsala Tita Street, the troops had moved in, and the Court has a great idea of the number of troops that there were and what they were doing in and around the Marsala Tita Street on that day, and yet he claims that he was able to move around unseen and to see Dusko Tadic at the triangle with Goran Borovnica assaulting one of the policemen held there, a policeman called Alic. How do we test the reliability of his evidence? Again, we can go back to his previous statement where he claimed that Goran Borovnica hit the particular policeman with a rifle. Again, we can look at what he described as what was happening down at the triangle. He claimed that people were being diverted to Prijedor and Trnopolje, but we have other evidence that, in fact, that was all happening elsewhere than at the triangle, but at the Limenka bus station further down on the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway. If he was able to move around Kozarac with a kalashnikov dressed as he was and avoid detection by the military that were taking over Kozarac at that time, that would be very surprising, being so close to the centre of that town. How did he manage it? We submit that again he has not told the truth about this, but he is linking himself to certain incidents. When cross-examined, and these flaws in his evidence were pointed out to him concerning the account he had given previously, he claimed to have seen another incident elsewhere in Kozarac where beatings were taking place by Dusko Tadic of other policemen. Is this a witness who is prepared on his feet to make up a story to serve his own ends? We submit that that was a classic example of him doing that. There were a number of exaggerations and we would say he is, perhaps, a fantasist concerning his evidence. He described himself as part of an armed brigade escaping capture; that he was destroying checkpoints with a Captain Cirkin. They had plans to liberate Trnopolje. I have also given the examples of extreme killings concerning a child pierced with a rake, a man against a door with a knife and the head on a bayonet. We ask the Court to look with great care at this witness's testimony, and the flaws that have been exposed within it, we submit, provide a considerable doubt as to the basis of his account and the logic of what he is saying does not follow. But there we are. He came to give evidence, and this is one of the problems that Professor Wladimiroff has stressed in his opening, people will be prepared to come to this Court to give accounts. This is a very unusual case and unusual trial. It does not happen in ordinary circumstances, and the emotions and the loss to many are so great that, perhaps, there may almost be a compulsion for certain witnesses not to assist this Court with genuine evidence. This witness also -- I will deal with him now in relation to two other matters -- claimed to have seen Dusko Tadic at Keraterm. It is interesting that, in fact, there were only four witnesses in this whole case who claimed to have seen Dusko Tadic at Keraterm, and he was one of them in a room of 572 people. His usual place was the far right-hand corner of room 2. He claimed, in those circumstances, to have been able to have seen Dusko Tadic at some considerable distance away. Perhaps the flavour of his evidence can be taken from the fact that he said he went into a van that was taking prisoners, not on the Banja Luka road, but to Kozarac and Omarska. That may, indeed, give a flavour of this witness and perhaps the way he is prepared to paint a picture in a certain way. There is no way he would have known a van was going to Omarska. He gave no explanation for why he should say that. The van would be going on the Banja Luka road if his evidence was to be taken, perhaps, to be right. His second sighting, and it is difficult for the Defence to deal with sightings without dates. It is quite apparent it is easy for anyone to say they have seen someone and maybe you can say, "No, you did not", maybe they can say, "Yes, I did", but it is difficult with sightings to try to pierce into that evidence. We submit the Court will have a very heavy task, a tough task, in relation to evidence such as this in having to weigh up whether it is genuine testimony or not. But it is interesting that of the sightings in Keraterm (of which there were only four witnesses) it also includes Witness Q. Moving on back to Kozarac and the attack on Kozarac, paragraph 4.1 of the indictment deals with this period between 24th to 27th May. After the incident at the triangle when it was alleged that Dusko Tadic beat one of the policemen standing there at the same time as Goran Borovnica, the next sighting is by the witness Azra Blazevic in the afternoon of that day. The Court will remember her testimony well -- I think she has been a witness often referred to here -- and what amounts to a brief fleeting glance of a lady standing one side of the triangle observing a figure passing the other side of the triangle for a short period of time which she is convinced, because of a remark made at the time, was Dusko Tadic. We ask the Court to consider those matters relating to identification evidence and whether this evidence is reliable or not and the particular sighting, the circumstances, the period of time to judge whether this is indeed a correct sighting or what we submit has all the capability of being a mistaken sighting. We say that because of the vast range of activity that Dusko Tadic was supposed to be undertaking on 26th May within Kozarac. I will come to those details in a moment. On 26th May he is also seen at Keraterm ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me Mr. Kay before you leave that, the Defence offered a photograph, a group of photographs from Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was that designed to relate to this instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It was the photographs from the pastry shop across the triangle?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and the progress across that triangle. The photograph was taken from the position where she would have been according to her testimony. Also on this day, and the Prosecution in their closing address through Miss Hollis said that this involved a part of the preparatory conduct of Dusko Tadic before he went to Kozarac, but Witness S on whom they seem to place great reliance apparently saw this man, Dusko Tadic, in the morning of 26th May at Keraterm. Again, one sets that against the alleged sighting by Witness Q of the morning of 26th May, and one wonders quite how this Defendant was supposed to have achieved so much on one day, given what the Court will appreciate must have been a military operation with people with specific tasks and duties that would have been controlled by captains or lieutenants or colonels and people having a job to do. But there it is. On the morning of 26th May Witness S puts the Defendant Dusko Tadic at Keraterm. Witness Q puts him at the triangle on the morning of 26th May. So we move from there with those matters to the witness Seferovic who gave evidence about the church killings on the morning of 26th May. As he had come back into the town and fed his birds and moved through the back gardens of various houses, he claimed, to get to the orchard and to peer through the bushes and, as he alleged, see Dusko Tadic with part of a group of military men slitting the throat of the chief of police of Kozarac, Osman, and also of another policeman called Adem Besic. At some stage I suppose sightings stop, but this is all on the morning of 26th May, given these numbers of people moving around Kozarac and in a military situation. This Court is in a dilemma, we submit. The Prosecution put reliance on Witness S and the Keraterm sighting. Quite what was he doing there, what was his role, what was his function? They have also called the evidence of Seferovic, the man with the birds, as well as Witness Q. If Seferovic had seen what he saw, the slitting of men's throats from the front, one would have expected Dusko Tadic to have been soaked in blood on that day. There has been no mention of that from the witnesses. When that witness Seferovic went to feed his birds, went down to his brother's house not far from the church and proceeded through the backs of the houses, why was he going there? What was he doing? What was the purpose? The previous periods he had left Kozarac, everyone knew Kozarac was a danger. He left Kozarac. He went away. He only made fleeting visits into that town. Why was he going further down into trouble? He was not going to go to a collection centre, he was not going to give himself up, if he is telling the truth about what he saw, or is this a made-up story by a man perhaps who knew the relatives and family of the victims, and is trying to do his bit for them? Certainly, if all these witnesses are to be believed about these sightings, someone somewhere cannot be right about that morning of 26th May. Someone has to be making it up within the Prosecution case. The Defence case is Dusko Tadic was not there, that he did not do those things. The other sighting on 26th May within Kozarac itself was as I referred to, the triangle and Azra Blazevic seeing him there in the afternoon and I have addressed the Court on that matter. There is the further sighting by the witness Mujic of Dusko Tadic being on a tank in Marsala Tita Street. He did not give a time for it. He gave an account which varied with a previous statement, which claimed that Dusko Tadic was riding a tank through Kozarac, perhaps in very dramatic fashion. This account that he gave before the Court was that he was just on the tank and, for some reason, one knows not why, he said that he hit a small boy on the head or cuffed him on the ear. Quite why and for what purpose one does not know, and there was no explanation about that. Also during this period, slightly outside Kozarac but probably still part of it, there is the Limenka bus station sighting by Mehmed Alic who gives evidence also on paragraph 6. He had gone from the place where he lived with his daughter, not Nasiha Klipic who gave evidence but another daughter, and his wife. He thought it was probably in the morning, but he went to Limenka and that was where there was division of prisoners at that place, some being sent to Prijedor, some to Trnopolje. He claimed to have seen Dusko Tadic there. Yet another job. Yet another function. Yet another role. We submit again that this may well be a fabricated account. I say that with great respect to a man who has suffered the losses that he has, but we have our job to do on behalf of the Defence to point out matters in evidence to the Court and sometimes we cannot do it other than in a blunt way. Anything less may be taken as being less than convincing. But it is interesting that he claims that sighting at Limenka on 26th May where people are being divided, because on 27th May his daughter Nasiha Klipic also claims that she saw Dusko Tadic, not at Limenka but at Zikina's being part of the forces taking people on to the buses for them to be taken to either Prijedor, Trnopolje or elsewhere. She had also claimed a sighting before Zikina's whilst on her way, whilst travelling in the convoy down the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway. That was when she claimed she saw Dusko Tadic in a car being driven by a policeman called Brane Balte, probably not far from Limenka's where the father claims to have seen Dusko Tadic on that day on 26th May. It does seem an odd coincidence that these two witnesses who are related see, apparently, Dusko Tadic on different days at the various bus stations where they are sent off. Of all the witnesses passing through Limenka and Zikina's on this day of 26th/27th May they are the only ones who claim sightings there. Many other witnesses have been called to give evidence, and I will give the Court some of the names for 26th May: Hamdija Kahrimanovic, Kemal Susic, Halid Mujkanovic, Muharem Besic, Husein Hodzic, Ermin Strikovic. On 27th May passing through Limenka or Zikina's were Ferid Mujcic, Salko Karabasic, Sulejman Besic, Sefik Kesic, Adil Jakupovic, Nasiha Jakupovic, Bahrija Denic, Eniz Besic and Witness H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I understand the latter part of your very reasoned submission. I do not understand why it is an odd coincidence that father and daughter should see at slightly different places the accused performing a similar task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Our submission is it is an odd coincidence that it is these two witnesses who are related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And no one else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And no one else who see this, and so many people pass through and do not refer to Dusko Tadic being there. Conversely, if they are right and he was part of the group separating people down at the Limenka and Zikina's on these days, what else was he doing? One has reasonably to draw the line in relation to all these functions and jobs that he is doing on 26th May 27th May which is surprisingly of a very different nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So the coincidence that you are pointing out is not so much that father and daughter see him, but that they say they see him and no one else does?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, I follow. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am using irony there perhaps which sometimes works, sometimes does not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understood you!

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Also on that day of 27th May, and I am moving to that date now having touched on the sightings of Nasiha Klipic at about 4.00 p.m. on the afternoon of that day, Witness S again apparently sees Dusko Tadic at Keraterm. He gave his evidence about that. So again it is not only one day where these apparent division of roles, multiplicity of tasks, we say, call into question the reliability of this evidence; it is also the next day. I will turn now to Nasiha Klipic's evidence. The Court may remember her account of coming down in this poor bedraggled convoy from Vidovici through Kozarac, down on to the new highway, and whilst on a cart she described seeing a car being driven by the man Brane Balte with Dusko Tadic in the front passenger seat, someone else in the back of the car, but going in the opposite direction from the way she was travelling; going towards Kozarac. The next account that she gives is arriving at Zikina's tavern and seeing Dusko Tadic there directing or being part of the group of soldiers separating people into buses. Again, how on earth, if he is travelling one way, would he have got back to the site at Zikina's? Unless she had missed him in the traffic or something like that, but she gave particular evidence that she was looking out for police officers because her husband had been a policeman and she felt that on that particular day someone in the police might help her in her unfortunate circumstances. These two areas of Zikina's and Limenka's bus stops are not far apart.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, was there not evidence given as to the time though that she had seen him, both when he passed her and also when she saw him at the bus station? I thought that the Prosecution had specifically asked for times on that and the length of the column, I thought, I guess I would have to go back to the transcript ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it actually came from cross-examination, your Honour. I was asking about the times and she arrived at Zikina's at 4.00 p.m. She was at the front of this column that had come down from Vidovici or near the front, and that is how she remained. There was a series of questions from me which may have been painful for the Court at the time and I was conscious I was taking time and no one might have appreciated what I was doing, but it was this front of the column that was moving down and she remained near the front throughout the whole of this journey she undertook.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought it was from another witness, but I will have to go back and check. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The actual location of the place where they were sorting out the men and the women, was that near Susici or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Which is, according to my notation on Exhibit 280, on the old road, but it was in fact on the new road?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is on the new road, the asphalt road as they call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course, one immediately imagines that the accused might have gone back on the old road, but there does not seem to be any cross-over between the two. I do not really know where the locations are, the two that you have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard testimony that ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: They are not shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- Zikina's was about -- no -- was about one and a half kilometres from where the head of the Kozarac Marsala Tita Street joins the ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- intersection. We are not talking great distances at all. We put this before the Court as a curious dilemma. If he going one way, presumably to do something or to be involved in something, how is it that when she arrives he is already involved in doing something, which is apparently the separation of the people? For what it is worth, and I am not making a big point on this, in her previous statement she had said that Dusko Tadic was giving the orders to people, but in her evidence she said another man was giving the orders and Dusko Tadic was one of those who was accepting the orders, dividing people and putting them on the various buses. But this is a problem within the Prosecution case, because there must be some logic to what is going on on this day which would have been planned and which the military people appeared to know what they were doing. How on earth could he be in two different places at the same time? I will turn now to the other important allegation on 27th May, which will have to go into closed session with the sound turned off. I do not know if your Honour wants me to start that tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please turn off -- any objection from the Prosecution, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. We will turn off the sound please and we will go into closed session.
